title: Inside a cell: why your cells need a transport system and a bacterium does not

summary.text: Your cells need a transport system inside them, but a tiny bacterium does not. Why? In this unit you will time how far colour drifts into a potato over 1, 4 and 16 hours, walk a coin to see wandering against walking straight, and send proteins to the right place in a cell.
summary.art: A small rod-shaped bacterium beside a much larger animal cell cut open to show folded bags, a stack of flat bags, round parcels moving along thin tracks, and bean-shaped mitochondria the same size as the bacterium.

intro.hook: A bacterium is alive. She eats, grows and makes copies of herself. Yet she has no nucleus, no Golgi body, no lysosomes and no tracks. Your cells have all of them. So what are these parts for, if a living cell can do without them? Say what you think, and why.
intro.text: Here is one clue. A bacterium is about 2 micrometres long. A micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre. A cell from your skin is about 20 micrometres wide, so she is ten times as wide as the bacterium. In the Potato Colour Test you will find out what that extra size does to a cell. You will measure how far colour drifts in 1 hour, 4 hours and 16 hours. The answer explains why your cells have tracks and motors, and it is a clue to the other parts too.
intro.art: A child looking at a tiny rod-shaped bacterium drawn next to a large round cell, with a ruler marked in micrometres under both.

outcomes: By the end I can explain, with my potato results, why drifting is quick over a short distance and slow over a long one.
By the end I can follow a protein from a ribosome through the rough ER and the Golgi body to the outside of the cell.
By the end I can explain how a protein reaches the right place in a cell with nobody directing it.
By the end I can say what lysosomes and peroxisomes do, and why a lysosome is acidic inside.
By the end I can name the three kinds of fibre in the cytoskeleton and say how motor proteins carry cargo.
By the end I can compare a bacterial cell with one of my own cells: what both have, and what differs.
By the end I can give four pieces of evidence that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria.
By the end I can tell apart what scientists have shown about cells and what they still argue about.

terms.meaning: A micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre. Scientists measure cells in micrometres.
terms.example: A hair from your head is about 70 micrometres thick. A bacterium is about 2 micrometres long.
terms.art: A single hair drawn very large, with a tiny rod-shaped bacterium next to the hair and a scale bar.

terms.meaning: Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a place with many of them to a place with few. It happens because particles are always being knocked about by their neighbours.
terms.example: The smell of sambar reaches the next room by diffusion and by moving air.
terms.art: A drop of colour in still water, with dots spreading outward from the drop.

terms.meaning: A prokaryote is a living being whose cell has no nucleus. Bacteria are prokaryotes. Almost all of them are single cells.
terms.example: The bacteria who turn milk into curd are prokaryotes.
terms.art: A rod-shaped cell with a loop of DNA lying loose inside and no nucleus.

terms.meaning: A eukaryote is a living being whose cells have a nucleus and other parts wrapped in membranes. Animals, plants, fungi and amoebas are eukaryotes.
terms.example: You, a coconut palm, a mushroom and the yeast in bread dough are all eukaryotes.
terms.art: A cell with a nucleus, mitochondria and folded bags inside, next to a person, a palm and a mushroom.

terms.meaning: The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of flat bags and tubes of membrane, joined to the skin of the nucleus. Rough ER carries ribosomes and makes proteins. Smooth ER has no ribosomes and makes fats.
terms.example: Cells of the pancreas, which make digestive enzymes all day, are packed with rough ER.
terms.art: Folded flat bags dotted with ribosomes around a nucleus, leading into smooth tubes with no dots.

terms.meaning: The Golgi body is a stack of about four to eight flat bags of membrane. It finishes proteins that come from the ER, adds sugar tags and sorts them by where they must go.
terms.example: A cell that makes mucus in your nose has a large Golgi body, because mucus proteins need many sugars added.
terms.art: A stack of curved flat bags with small bubbles arriving on one side and leaving on the other.

terms.meaning: A vesicle is a tiny bubble of membrane that carries cargo inside a cell. It pinches off from one membrane and joins another.
terms.example: Insulin waits inside vesicles in a pancreas cell until your blood sugar rises.
terms.art: A small bubble pinching off from a flat bag, and another bubble joining the cell's outer membrane.

terms.meaning: A signal label is a short stretch of a protein's own chain, or a tag added to it, that says where in the cell the protein belongs. Scientists call it a signal sequence.
terms.example: A protein with a nucleus label is carried through a pore into the nucleus. A protein with no label stays where it was made.
terms.art: A long folded chain with one short end coloured differently, and a parcel tag tied to that end.

terms.meaning: Secretion is the sending of a substance out of a cell. A vesicle joins the cell membrane and empties its cargo outside.
terms.example: Your salivary glands secrete saliva when you smell lemon rice.
terms.art: A vesicle joined to the edge of a cell, opening to the outside and letting small dots out.

terms.meaning: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up one chemical change. Each enzyme works on one kind of molecule and comes out unchanged, ready to work again.
terms.example: An enzyme in your saliva cuts starch from rice into sugar.
terms.art: A large protein with a notch, holding a long chain and cutting it into two pieces.

terms.meaning: A lysosome is a small bag of membrane that holds about fifty kinds of digesting enzymes in acid. It takes apart worn-out cell parts and things the cell has swallowed.
terms.example: A white blood cell swallows a bacterium and joins the bag to a lysosome, where the bacterium is digested.
terms.art: A round bag with small scissors inside, joined to a larger bag that holds a worn-out mitochondrion.

terms.meaning: Autophagy is a cell's way of wrapping her own worn-out parts in a membrane and sending them to a lysosome. The pieces are used again. The word means self-eating.
terms.example: When you have not eaten for many hours, your liver cells recycle more of their own parts by autophagy.
terms.art: A double membrane closing round an old mitochondrion, then joining a lysosome.

terms.meaning: A peroxisome is a small bag of enzymes that breaks down fats and destroys hydrogen peroxide. Hydrogen peroxide is a harmful chemical that cells make as they work.
terms.example: Potato cells and liver cells both have many peroxisomes, so both make hydrogen peroxide fizz.
terms.art: A small round bag with bubbles of oxygen rising from it.

terms.meaning: The cytoskeleton is the network of protein fibres inside a cell. It gives the cell her shape, lets her move and gives motor proteins tracks to walk on.
terms.example: A white blood cell crawls after a bacterium by building new fibres at her front edge.
terms.art: A cell outline filled with a web of thin fibres, with thicker tubes spreading out from near the nucleus.

terms.meaning: A microtubule is a hollow tube built from a protein called tubulin. It is the thickest fibre of the cytoskeleton, and it is the main track for long-distance cargo.
terms.example: Microtubules run the whole length of the nerve cell that reaches from your lower back to your toes.
terms.art: A hollow tube made of small beads, with beads being added at one end.

terms.meaning: An actin filament is a thin fibre built from a protein called actin. Actin filaments lie mostly under the cell membrane, and they push and pull it.
terms.example: Your muscles shorten when the motor protein myosin pulls on actin filaments.
terms.art: Two thin strands twisted together under the edge of a cell, pushing the edge outward.

terms.meaning: A motor protein is a protein that walks along a fibre of the cytoskeleton, carrying cargo. Each step uses the energy of one ATP. ATP is the small molecule that carries energy in every cell.
terms.example: The motor protein kinesin takes about a hundred steps a second along a microtubule.
terms.art: A protein with two feet walking along a tube, carrying a large round bubble on its back.

terms.meaning: Endosymbiosis is one living being living inside the cells of another, with both gaining from it. Mitochondria and chloroplasts began this way.
terms.example: The bacteria in the root swellings of a groundnut plant live inside her cells and make nitrogen food for her.
terms.art: A large cell with a smaller, different cell living inside it, with arrows showing each giving something to the other.

explanations.concept: Diffusion: drifting is quick over a short distance and slow over a long one
explanations.definition: Diffusion is the spreading of particles from where there are many to where there are few. To drift twice as far takes about four times as long.
explanations.description: Every molecule in water is moving, and neighbours bump it billions of times each second. Each bump sends it a new way, so the molecule wanders. Wandering covers a tiny distance quickly. But the time grows much faster than the distance. Twice as far takes about four times as long. Ten times as far takes about a hundred times as long. You saw this in the Potato Colour Test: after sixteen times the time, the colour was only about four times as deep. Now think about cells. A small protein drifts across a bacterium in a small fraction of a second. Across one of your skin cells, ten times as wide, it needs a few seconds. That is still quick enough. But a vesicle full of proteins is far bigger than one protein, and the crowded inside of a cell holds it back. Drifting could take it hours. And a nerve cell can be a metre long. Drifting from one end to the other would take hundreds of years. So a large cell does not rely on drifting for her large cargo. She carries it.
examples: In the Potato Colour Test, the colour went about twice as deep in 4 hours as in 1 hour, not four times as deep.
In the Coin Walk, a token that wanders needs about 9 tosses to get 3 squares away and about 36 tosses to get 6 squares away.
A drop of ink in a still tumbler reaches the water next to it in seconds. Without stirring or currents, it would take weeks to colour the whole tumbler evenly.
explanations.art: Three pieces of potato cut open, with a coloured rim 2, 4 and 8 millimetres deep, labelled 1 hour, 4 hours and 16 hours.

explanations.concept: The route of a protein: rough ER, Golgi body, vesicle
explanations.definition: A protein that will leave the cell is made on the rough ER, finished and sorted in the Golgi body, and carried to the cell membrane in a vesicle.
explanations.description: A ribosome is the small machine that builds a protein by joining amino acids into a chain. If the protein is for export, the ribosome sits on the rough ER and feeds the growing chain inside. There, helper proteins fold the chain into its working shape. A chain that folds wrongly is held back, and if it cannot be mended it is taken apart. This checking matters, because a wrongly folded protein can stick to others and harm the cell. A vesicle then pinches off the ER and carries the protein to the Golgi body. The Golgi body has a receiving side and a sending side. As the protein passes through, enzymes add and trim sugars. On the sending side, proteins are sorted into different vesicles by their labels. The vesicle joins the cell membrane and the protein is outside. The smooth ER has no ribosomes. It makes the fats for new membrane, and in your liver it changes medicines and poisons so the body can remove them.
examples: Collagen is the most plentiful protein in your body. It is the strong rope between cells in skin, bone and tendon. In 1954, G. N. Ramachandran and Gopinath Kartha at the University of Madras worked out that collagen is three chains wound together. Cells fold those three chains inside the rough ER.
Insulin is made in the pancreas, packed into vesicles and kept ready. When your blood sugar rises after a meal, the vesicles join the membrane and let the insulin out.
One cell that makes antibodies can send out thousands of antibody molecules every second. She is almost filled with rough ER.
explanations.art: A protein chain passing from a ribosome into a folded bag, then inside a bubble to a stack of flat bags, then in a second bubble to the cell's edge and out.

explanations.concept: How a protein finds its place: the label is part of the protein
explanations.definition: A protein carries its own address. The address is a short stretch of its chain, or a tag added to it, and machines in the cell read it.
explanations.description: A cell makes thousands of kinds of protein, and each kind belongs in one place. No part of the cell holds a list of where everything goes. Each protein carries its own label. In the 1970s, Günter Blobel and his colleagues showed that a protein for export begins with a short signal stretch. A particle in the cell holds on to that stretch and brings the ribosome to the ER. Other labels send a protein into the nucleus or into a mitochondrion. A protein with no label stays in the watery part of the cell where it was made. Enzymes for the lysosome get a sugar tag in the Golgi body. In 1972, Elizabeth Neufeld and Scot Hickman studied children with a rare illness called I-cell disease. Their cells made the lysosome enzymes correctly, but sent them out of the cell. Neufeld and Hickman proposed that the enzymes were missing a tag. Later work found the tag and proved them right. Vesicles carry labels too. Matching proteins on a vesicle and on its target membrane fit together, and only then do the two membranes join.
examples: Haemoglobin has no label, so it stays in the watery part of the young red blood cell that makes it.
The proteins that DNA winds around carry a nucleus label, so they are taken in through the pores of the nucleus.
James Rothman, Randy Schekman and Thomas Südhof shared a Nobel Prize in 2013 for showing how vesicles find the right membrane and join it.
explanations.art: Four folded proteins, each with a differently coloured tag, heading to four places in a cell: the nucleus, a mitochondrion, a lysosome and the outside.

explanations.concept: Lysosomes: bags of enzymes that work only in acid
explanations.definition: A lysosome is a bag of digesting enzymes kept in acid. It breaks large molecules into small ones, and the cell uses those again.
explanations.description: Every part of a cell wears out. A mitochondrion lasts a few weeks. Many proteins last only hours or days. A cell that only built and never took apart would fill up with broken parts. Lysosomes do the taking apart. Each holds about fifty kinds of enzyme, and each enzyme cuts one kind of large molecule: proteins, fats, starch-like chains or DNA. Why do these enzymes not digest the cell herself? The enzymes work well only in acid. The cell pumps acid into the lysosome, so the inside is about as sour as tomato juice. The rest of the cell is not sour. If a little enzyme leaks out, it almost stops working. The bag's own membrane is protected on the inside by a coat of sugars. Worn parts reach the lysosome by autophagy. The cell wraps the old part in a membrane, and that parcel joins a lysosome. The small molecules that come out are used to build new parts. Yoshinori Ohsumi worked out the steps of autophagy in yeast cells in the 1990s.
examples: When a tadpole becomes a frog, lysosomes help to digest the cells of the tail. The tadpole uses the material to build legs.

Some children are born without one working lysosome enzyme. The molecule it should cut piles up in their cells and makes them ill. Doctors can now treat a few of these illnesses by giving the missing enzyme.
A white blood cell that has swallowed a bacterium joins the bag to a lysosome, and the enzymes digest the bacterium.
explanations.art: A round bag labelled 'acid inside', with small enzymes cutting a long chain into short pieces that pass out into the cell.

explanations.concept: Peroxisomes: small bags that deal with a harmful chemical
explanations.definition: A peroxisome is a small bag of enzymes that breaks down fats and destroys hydrogen peroxide.
explanations.description: When a cell breaks down fats, one of the products is hydrogen peroxide. Hydrogen peroxide damages proteins and DNA, so the cell must not let it spread. The cell does this work inside peroxisomes. A peroxisome holds an enzyme called catalase. Catalase turns hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas as fast as it is made. One catalase molecule can deal with millions of hydrogen peroxide molecules every second. In the Fizzing Potato test, the bubbles are oxygen made by catalase from potato cells. Why keep this work in a separate bag? The harmful chemical is made and destroyed in the same small space, so very little of it reaches the rest of the cell.
examples: Raw potato, raw liver and even a drop of blood make hydrogen peroxide fizz, because all of them contain catalase.
Boiled potato does not fizz. Heat changes the shape of an enzyme, and an enzyme with the wrong shape no longer works.
The foam on a cut cleaned with hydrogen peroxide is oxygen, made by catalase from your own cells.
explanations.art: A small round bag inside a cell, with an arrow showing hydrogen peroxide going in and water and oxygen bubbles coming out.

explanations.concept: The cytoskeleton: three kinds of fibre that are always being rebuilt
explanations.definition: The cytoskeleton is a network of three kinds of protein fibre: actin filaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules. A cell builds and takes apart most of these fibres all the time.
explanations.description: Your bones were built once and stay for years. A cell's skeleton is different. Actin filaments are the thinnest fibres. They lie under the cell membrane and push it out or pull it in. A crawling white blood cell builds actin at her front and takes it apart at her back. Microtubules are hollow tubes and the thickest fibres. Most of them grow outward from a spot near the nucleus. In 1984, Tim Mitchison and Marc Kirschner found that a microtubule grows steadily and then suddenly shrinks. Most microtubules last only a few minutes. Why would a cell keep building tracks and breaking them? Because she can then change shape, move or divide within minutes, using the same building blocks again. Intermediate filaments are the third kind. They are the lasting ones, like ropes, and they stop the cell being torn when she is stretched. Your hair and nails are made of an intermediate filament protein called keratin, left behind by cells that have died.
examples: When a cell divides, she takes apart her microtubules and rebuilds them into the frame that pulls the two sets of chromosomes apart.
The tiny hairs that sweep dust out of your windpipe are bundles of microtubules, bent to and fro by motor proteins.
Skin cells are tied to each other by keratin ropes. That is why skin can stretch over a bent knee without tearing.
explanations.art: One cell drawn three times, showing thin fibres under the membrane, rope-like fibres across the cell, and tubes spreading out from near the nucleus.

explanations.concept: Motor proteins: carrying cargo along the tracks
explanations.definition: A motor protein walks along a fibre of the cytoskeleton and carries cargo. Each step uses one ATP.
explanations.description: In 1985, Ronald Vale, Thomas Reese and Michael Sheetz found a motor protein in the giant nerve cells of squid. They named it kinesin. Kinesin has two feet. One foot holds the microtubule while the other swings forward, and each step is 8 millionths of a millimetre. Kinesin can take about a hundred steps a second. A microtubule has two different ends, so a motor knows which way to walk. Most kinesins walk outward, towards the edge of the cell. Another motor, dynein, walks inward. A vesicle often carries both kinds, and it moves in the direction of the side that is pulling harder. At about one micrometre a second, a motor crosses an ordinary cell in under a minute. At that speed, the trip down a nerve cell one metre long takes about twelve days. Drifting would take hundreds of years. In Mumbai, Roop Mallik and his group have studied how several motors share one load, like people carrying a heavy cot together.
examples: A pigment cell in the skin of a fish or a frog moves her grains of colour outward or inward along microtubules. This changes how dark the skin looks within minutes.
In your muscles, the motor protein myosin pulls on actin filaments. Millions of these small pulls add up to lifting your school bag.
Some viruses fix themselves to a cell's motor proteins and are carried to the nucleus.
Every step of a motor protein is paid for with ATP. ATP was found in muscle in 1929 by Cyrus Fiske and Yellapragada Subbarow, who was born in Bhimavaram in Andhra Pradesh.
explanations.art: A two-footed motor protein walking along a tube towards the edge of a cell, carrying a round vesicle much bigger than itself.

explanations.concept: A bacterial cell compared with one of your cells
explanations.definition: A bacterium is a prokaryote: a small cell with no nucleus and no organelles wrapped in membrane. Your cells are eukaryote cells: about ten times as wide, with a nucleus and many organelles.
explanations.description: A bacterium and one of your cells share the basic equipment of life. Both have a cell membrane, DNA, ribosomes and ATP, and both read DNA with the same code. The differences follow from size and from history. A bacterium is about 1 to 2 micrometres long. Her DNA is usually one ring that lies in the watery inside of the cell. Her ribosomes are a little smaller than yours and have a different shape. Most bacteria have a tough cell wall outside the membrane. She makes ATP on her own cell membrane. Because she is so small, molecules reach every part of her by drifting. So she lives well without a transport system. With plenty of food she can copy herself in 20 minutes. Your cells keep their DNA in a nucleus, make ATP inside mitochondria, and move large cargo by vesicle and motor. Medicines use the differences. Penicillin stops bacteria building their wall, and your cells have no wall. Other antibiotics jam bacterial ribosomes and leave yours alone. In 2000, Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, who was born in Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu, and his group showed exactly where such antibiotics sit on the bacterial ribosome.
examples: The bacteria in curd, the bacteria on your skin and the bacteria in soil are all prokaryotes.
Yeast is a single cell, but she is a eukaryote. She has a nucleus and mitochondria, as your cells do.
Bacteria do some chemistry that no animal or plant cell can do. Some take nitrogen from the air. Some live on iron or sulphur.
explanations.art: A rod-shaped bacterium and an animal cell drawn to the same scale, with shared parts in one colour and different parts in another.

explanations.concept: Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria: the evidence
explanations.definition: Mitochondria come from bacteria that began to live inside a larger cell about two billion years ago. Chloroplasts come from other bacteria that could use sunlight.
explanations.description: This idea sounds unlikely, so look at the evidence. First, a mitochondrion has her own DNA, and it is a ring, as in bacteria. Second, she has her own ribosomes, and they are like bacterial ribosomes. A few antibiotics that jam bacterial ribosomes also disturb mitochondria. Third, a cell cannot make a mitochondrion from nothing. New mitochondria come only from old ones, which grow and split in two, as bacteria do. Fourth, she has two membranes, and she makes ATP on the inner one, as a bacterium does on her own membrane. Fifth, she is the size of a bacterium. Sixth, when scientists read the DNA of mitochondria, it matched one group of living bacteria. But a mitochondrion can no longer live alone. Over time, most of her genes moved into the cell's nucleus. Your mitochondria hold only 37 genes. The cell makes more than a thousand kinds of protein for them and sends these in with a mitochondrion label. Lynn Margulis argued for this history in 1967, against most biologists of her time.
examples: In 1966, Kwang Jeon's laboratory amoebas were infected by bacteria. Most died. After many generations of amoebas, the survivors could not live without those bacteria. A harmful guest had become a needed partner while scientists watched.
An amoeba called Paulinella took in a sunlight-using bacterium about a hundred million years ago. This happened separately from the plants.
In 2024, scientists reported a sea alga whose nitrogen-catching bacterium has become a true part of the cell. It is the first known organelle that takes nitrogen from the air.
explanations.art: A mitochondrion and a free-living bacterium side by side at the same size, each with a ring of DNA and small ribosomes inside.

explanations.concept: Which came first: the large cell or the mitochondrion?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that mitochondria were once bacteria. They do not agree on what the host cell was like when the two met.
explanations.description: Nobody watched it happen, and the first such cells left almost no fossils. So scientists reason from living cells and their DNA. The host belonged to a group of microbes called archaea. They are small cells with no nucleus, but they are not bacteria. The argument is about the order of events.
examples: If the large cell came first, there should once have been large cells with a skeleton and no mitochondria. No such cell has been found alive today.

In 2020, Hiroyuki Imachi and his team reported that they had grown a close relative of the host. It took them twelve years. She is a tiny cell with long arms, and she lives closely beside partner microbes.

perspectives.explanation: The host had already become large, with a skeleton that let her swallow other cells. One day she swallowed a bacterium and did not digest her. In this view the skeleton made the mitochondrion possible.

perspectives.who: Mitochondrion first (Nick Lane and William Martin, among others)
perspectives.explanation: The host was still small. A bacterium came to live inside her without being swallowed. The extra ATP from the new partners let the cell grow large and build a skeleton and a transport system. In this view the mitochondrion made the large cell possible.
The relatives of the host already have a few skeleton proteins and long arms. Perhaps the host slowly wrapped her arms round her partners. Then both changes happened together.

explanations.art: Two timelines side by side: in one a large cell swallows a bacterium, in the other a small cell with a bacterium inside grows large.

agreed.text: To drift twice as far by diffusion takes about four times as long.
agreed.evidence: Albert Einstein worked out this rule in 1905, and Jean Perrin confirmed it in 1908 by tracking tiny grains under a microscope. Your potato pieces show the same rule.

agreed.text: Proteins for export are made on the rough ER, pass through the Golgi body and leave the cell in vesicles.
agreed.evidence: In 1967, James Jamieson and George Palade gave pancreas cells radioactive amino acids for a few minutes. They then found the new proteins first over the rough ER, later in the Golgi body and last in vesicles at the cell's edge.

agreed.text: A protein carries its own address as part of itself.
agreed.evidence: Cut the signal stretch off a protein and it stays in the watery part of the cell. Join that stretch to a different protein and the cell sends the different protein to the ER.

agreed.text: The cytoskeleton is built and taken apart all the time.
agreed.evidence: Films of living cells with glowing tubulin show single microtubules growing and then shrinking within minutes.

agreed.text: Bacteria and our cells share the same basic chemistry and one ancestor.
agreed.evidence: Both use DNA, the same code for reading it, ribosomes and ATP. Hundreds of genes are similar in all living cells.

agreed.text: Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria.
agreed.evidence: They have their own ring of DNA and their own ribosomes of the bacterial kind. They form only by splitting, and their genes match living groups of bacteria.

challenging.claim: Bacteria have no skeleton and no compartments inside.
challenging.for: Under an ordinary microscope a bacterium looks like a plain bag. She has no nucleus and no membrane-wrapped organelles like ours.
challenging.against: In 1991, Erfei Bi and Joe Lutkenhaus found a ring of protein fibre that pinches a bacterium in two. That protein is a relative of our tubulin. In 2001, relatives of actin were found too. Some bacteria also build small compartments with protein walls.
challenging.context: This card is about an old statement in many books: that bacteria are plain bags with nothing organised inside.

challenging.claim: Bacteria are simple, early cells, and our cells are the advanced kind.
challenging.for: Our cells have many more parts, and they can build large bodies. Bacteria appeared on Earth first.
challenging.against: Today's bacteria have been changing for just as long as we have. They do chemistry no animal can do, and they live in boiling springs and deep rock. At her size, a bacterium is not missing a transport system, because drifting does that work. Each kind of cell fits a different way of living.
challenging.context: This card is about the habit of calling bacteria simple and our own cells advanced.

challenging.claim: A bacterium is always tiny and never has compartments for her DNA.
challenging.for: It is true for almost every bacterium studied.
challenging.against: In 2022, Jean-Marie Volland and colleagues described a bacterium from mangrove swamps in Guadeloupe who is about one centimetre long. You can see her without a microscope. She keeps her DNA in many small membrane bags. So a bacterium who is very large also has compartments.
challenging.context: This card is about a giant bacterium found in 2022, who breaks the usual rule that bacteria are tiny.

challenging.claim: The Golgi body is a row of fixed bags, and vesicles carry proteins from one bag to the next.
challenging.who: Many cell biologists, from the 1970s onward
challenging.for: Vesicles are seen budding from the edges of every bag in the stack.
challenging.against: Films of living yeast cells made in 2006 showed single bags changing over a few minutes from the receiving kind to the sending kind. So perhaps the bags themselves move through the stack, with the proteins inside them, and the vesicles carry enzymes backward. Both may happen.
challenging.context: This card is about how proteins pass through the Golgi body. Scientists still argue about it.

challenging.claim: A mitochondrion is still a bacterium, living inside us as a separate being.
challenging.who: Some writers and a few biologists
challenging.for: She has her own DNA and ribosomes, and she multiplies by splitting. She comes only from another mitochondrion.
challenging.against: She has passed almost all her genes to the nucleus and cannot live outside the cell for long. The cell decides when she divides and when she is recycled. Most biologists call her an organelle, a part of the cell.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a mitochondrion should be called a living being of her own or a part of the cell.

big_questions.q: A bacterium lives well with few parts, and your cells live well with many. Is one of these a better way to be alive?
big_questions.hint: What would 'better' mean here? Count how many bacteria there are, and how long they have lived on Earth.

big_questions.q: No part of a cell knows where every protein should go. Each protein carries its own label. Can something be well organised with nobody organising it?
big_questions.hint: Think of how a letter reaches a house. Does any one person know the whole route?

big_questions.q: A cell takes apart her own skeleton every few minutes and builds it again. Why might rebuilding be better than building something that lasts?
big_questions.hint: What can a white blood cell do that your thigh bone cannot?

big_questions.q: A mitochondrion cannot live without your cell, and your cell cannot live without her. Is that one living being or two?
big_questions.hint: Look at the evidence on each side: her own DNA, and the genes she has handed over.

big_questions.q: Your lysosomes take worn parts to pieces so that new parts can be built from them. Is taking apart a part of staying alive?
big_questions.hint: What would happen to a cell that only ever built?

big_questions.q: The word 'bacterium' covers a being one micrometre long and a being one centimetre long. What does a name tell us, and what does it hide?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the two have in common, and how differently they must live.

story.title: Six Digits
story.note: A made-up story. Thenmozhi, her mother and the night in the sorting hall are imagined, and children are not normally allowed into a sorting hall. The postal facts are real. India's six-digit PIN code began on 15 August 1972. The first digit names a large zone of the country, the first three together name a sorting district, and the last three name one post office. Madurai's head post office is 625001 and Shillong's is 793001. A letter that cannot be delivered or sent back goes to a Returned Letter Office.
text: The sorting hall behind Madurai railway station never slept. At ten at night its tube lights were all on, and the rain was loud on the tin roof.

Thenmozhi sat on an upturned crate with her school bag on her knees. She was ten. Her mother, Amudha, sorted letters here on the night shift. Tonight the neighbour who usually kept Thenmozhi had gone to a wedding in Dindigul, so Thenmozhi had come along. The supervisor had looked at her over his glasses and said nothing, which meant yes.

In her bag was a letter. She had written it three times before she liked it. It was for Ibadahun, who had sat beside her for two years and who had moved in June, with her whole family, back to Shillong. Thenmozhi had found Shillong on the map in her atlas. It was almost as far from Madurai as India went.

She looked round the hall. Sacks came in through one door and went out through another. Forty people stood at wooden frames full of small open boxes and flicked letters into them, fast, without seeming to look.
'Amma,' she said. 'Who here knows where Ibadahun's house is?'
Her mother did not stop sorting. 'Nobody.'
'Then who knows the way to Shillong?'
'Nobody here has been to Shillong, kanna.'

Thenmozhi held her bag tighter. She had imagined one person, somewhere at the back, with a great book of every lane in India. She had imagined giving the letter to that person. Now she looked at forty tired people and a leaking roof, and she wanted to take her letter home again.

Her mother glanced at her face. Then she pulled a tray of letters across the table. 'Come. Do this tray for me. You see my frame? Nine boxes on the top row, numbered one to nine. Look at the first digit of the PIN code on each letter. Only the first. Put the letter in the box with that number.'
'Only the first digit?'
'Only the first.'

The first letter said 600 028. Thenmozhi put it in box six. The next said 110 001, and went in box one. Then 682 011, box six again. 400 050, box four. It was easy. It was so easy that she became suspicious.
'But Amma, 600 028 and 682 011 are in the same box. One is Chennai and one is Kochi. Appa's sister lives in Kochi. They are not the same place.'

'They are the same zone. Six. The six bag gets opened again at another table, and there somebody reads the next two digits. Then it goes to a town, and somebody there reads the last three. And then a postman reads the street and the door number.' Her mother flicked four letters into four boxes. 'Each of us reads our own part. Nobody reads the whole thing.'

Thenmozhi sorted. A letter came up that had been out in the rain. The name had run into a blue cloud, and the street was gone. But the six digits stood in their six printed squares, a little blurred: 5 6 0 0 0 3. She showed her mother.
'Box five,' said her mother. 'It will get to Bengaluru. The last post office will work out the rest. They know their own streets.'

A few letters later, Thenmozhi stopped. This envelope was dry and clean. The handwriting was large and very careful, a child's. It said: To Paati, The Blue House, Near the Temple Tank. There was a stamp. There was no town. The six squares were empty.
She turned it over. Nothing on the back. She held it over box six, then box five, then put her hand down.
'Amma. Where does this one go?'

Her mother took it and read it, and her face went soft. 'Nowhere,' she said. 'Every town has a temple tank. This one cannot leave the hall.' She put it gently on a small pile at the end of the table. 'It goes to the Returned Letter Office. They will open it and look for a name inside. Sometimes they find one.'
'But the address is so neat.'
'It is very neat.'
Thenmozhi looked at the careful letters for a while. Whoever wrote them knew exactly where the blue house was. They had walked there. They had thought that was enough.
Then she opened her school bag very fast.

Her own envelope said Ibadahun's name, and the lane, and the big word SHILLONG, underlined twice. The six squares at the bottom were empty. She had not known what to put in them. She had thought the post office would know.
Her mother had already taken down a thick book with a soft, torn cover. She turned the pages with her thumb, the way she turned letters. 'Meghalaya. Shillong. Read it out.'
'Seven, nine, three, zero, zero, one.'
Thenmozhi wrote the digits in the squares, one in each, as large as they would go. Then she walked to her mother's frame by herself, and found the box with seven on it, and put the letter in.
story.epiphany: For the parent: nobody in the sorting hall knew the way to Shillong, and nobody needed to. The letter carried its own address, and each sorter read only one part of it. A cell works the same way. No part of a cell holds a list of where each protein belongs. Each protein carries a signal label as part of itself, and each machine along the route reads only that label. One difference is worth saying: a protein with no label is not sent back. It simply stays in the watery part of the cell where it was made.
ask: A letter with a smudged name but a clear PIN code can still travel. Why?
Nobody in the hall knew the whole route. How did letters still reach the right house?
A cell sends thousands of kinds of protein to the right places. What does each protein need to have?
In a cell, what happens to a protein that has no label at all?
Where else do things find their way with nobody directing them?

games.title: Bacterium, Your Cell or Both?
games.context: This is a card game about how a bacterial cell and one of your own cells are alike and different. Each card says one thing. You decide whether it is true of a bacterium, of your cell or of both, then turn the card over to check.

printables.title: 20 statement cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: She has a cell membrane all round her.
items.b: Both. Every living cell has a membrane that keeps her inside different from the outside.

items.f: She builds proteins on ribosomes.
items.b: Both. A bacterium's ribosomes are a little smaller than yours and shaped differently, but they do the same work.

items.f: She keeps her DNA inside a nucleus.
items.b: Your cell. A bacterium has no nucleus.

items.f: Her main DNA is one ring lying in the watery inside of the cell.
items.b: Bacterium. Your mitochondria keep a small ring like this too, which is a clue to where they came from.

items.f: She has mitochondria.
items.b: Your cell. A bacterium is about the size of one mitochondrion.

items.f: She uses ATP to carry energy.
items.b: Both. Every living cell on Earth uses ATP.

items.f: She is about 2 micrometres long.
items.b: Bacterium. More than a hundred of them in a row would fit across the full stop at the end of this sentence.

items.f: She is about 20 micrometres wide.
items.b: Your cell. That is about ten times as wide as a bacterium.

items.f: She has a Golgi body.
items.b: Your cell. A bacterium has no ER, no Golgi body and no lysosomes.

items.f: She moves vesicles along tracks with motor proteins.
items.b: Your cell. A bacterium is small enough for drifting to carry things everywhere inside her.

items.f: She has a tough wall outside her membrane, which penicillin stops her building.
items.b: Bacterium. Your cells have no wall, so penicillin leaves them alone.

items.f: With plenty of food she can copy herself in 20 minutes.
items.b: Bacterium. Your fastest-dividing cells need about half a day or more.

items.f: She has protein fibres that help her keep her shape and divide.
items.b: Both. For a long time books said bacteria had none. Relatives of tubulin and actin were found in bacteria in 1991 and 2001.

items.f: She reads her DNA with the same code as a banana plant does.
items.b: Both. Almost all living beings use the same code, which is strong evidence that they share one ancestor.

items.f: She is alive.
items.b: Both. Each one takes in food, uses energy, grows and makes more of herself.

items.f: She makes most of her ATP on her own cell membrane.
items.b: Bacterium. Your cells make most of theirs on the inner membrane of mitochondria.

items.f: She can swallow another whole cell.
items.b: Your cell. A white blood cell does this with her bendy membrane and her actin fibres. Almost no bacterium can.

items.f: She often carries small extra rings of DNA and can pass one to a neighbour.
items.b: Bacterium. The small rings are called plasmids.

items.f: She digests worn-out parts inside acid bags called lysosomes.
items.b: Your cell. A bacterium takes old proteins apart too, but with protein machines that float in her watery inside.

items.f: She is mostly water.
items.b: Both. The chemistry of every cell happens between molecules dissolved in water.

printables.title: Three answer slips for each player, to copy for up to four players

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, statement side up. Each player takes three answer slips: BACTERIUM, YOUR CELL and BOTH.
One player reads the top card aloud.
On the count of three, every player lays down one slip, face up.
Turn the card over and read the back. Every player with the right slip scores one point.
A player who can also give a reason, before the card is turned, scores one more point if the reason is right.
After 20 cards, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: lay down a slip for each card, then check. Try to reach 16 out of 20, then play again another day.

setup.art: A pile of statement cards on a table and three paper slips marked BACTERIUM, YOUR CELL and BOTH in front of each of two players.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a pile. Each player takes three answer slips.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while another player holds a slip ready, face down.
setup.caption: 2. Read the card. On the count of three, lay down one slip.

setup.art: A card turned over to show its answer, and a tally of points on a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. A right slip scores one point.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Write the three answer slips for each player. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, statement side up.
flow.say: Each card says one thing about a cell. We decide whether it is true of a bacterium, of one of our cells or of both.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Write three slips: BACTERIUM, YOUR CELL, BOTH. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bacterium, Your Cell or Both? Here you set up the cards and the answer slips.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Count to three. 3. Everyone lays down a slip. 4. Ask for reasons. 5. Turn the card over and read the back.
flow.say: Before we turn the card, tell me your reason. Is this about size, about parts or about something every cell needs?
flow.kid: Read the card. Lay down a slip. Say your reason. Turn the card and check.

ask.q: Which cards said BOTH, and what do they tell you?
good: A membrane, ribosomes, DNA, ATP and water are in both.
The things both have are the things every cell needs to stay alive.

flow.parent: The surprise cards are the fibres card and the cards that say BOTH. Children often expect a bacterium to share nothing with us. If your child puts YOUR CELL for everything, ask what a cell must have to stay alive at all.
flow.context: This is the main part of Bacterium, Your Cell or Both? Here you play through the 20 cards.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Sort the 20 cards into three heaps: BACTERIUM, YOUR CELL and BOTH. 3. Look at the YOUR CELL heap together. 4. Ask which of those parts are needed because the cell is large.
flow.say: Look at the heap of things only our cells have. Which of them does a cell need because she is large?
flow.kid: Count your points. Sort the cards into three heaps. Which parts does a large cell need?

check.q: A bacterium has no vesicles on tracks. How do molecules reach every part of her?
options: They drift, because she is so small
They do not need to move
Her nucleus sends them
check.why: A bacterium is about 2 micrometres long, and molecules drift that far in a small fraction of a second. Choosing 'her nucleus' forgets that a bacterium has no nucleus. Choosing 'do not need to move' forgets that every cell must bring molecules together for her chemistry.

flow.context: This is the last step of Bacterium, Your Cell or Both? Here you count the points and sort the cards into three heaps.

games.title: Label Post: send each protein to its place
games.context: This is a sorting game about how proteins reach the right place in a cell. Each card is a protein with its labels. You use a key to read the labels and send the protein to one of seven places.

printables.title: The label key and the seven places
items: No label: the protein stays in the WATERY INSIDE of the cell, where it was made.
Label N: the protein is carried into the NUCLEUS.
Label M: the protein is carried into a MITOCHONDRION.
Label E alone: the protein goes into the ER, through the Golgi body and OUT OF THE CELL.
Labels E and L: the protein goes into the ER, through the Golgi body and into a LYSOSOME.
Labels E and A: the protein goes into the ER and the Golgi body, and stays fixed in the CELL MEMBRANE.
Labels E and R: the protein goes into the ER and STAYS IN THE ER.

printables.title: 18 protein cards to cut out (the place is on the back)

items.f: INSULIN. A messenger protein made in the pancreas. It tells other cells to take in sugar. Label: E.
items.b: Out of the cell. Insulin waits in vesicles and is let out when blood sugar rises.

items.f: COLLAGEN. The strong rope protein that lies between the cells of skin and bone. Label: E.
items.b: Out of the cell. Collagen does its work outside cells, so it must be sent out.

items.f: ANTIBODY. A protein that sticks to germs in the blood. Label: E.
items.b: Out of the cell. One cell can send out thousands of antibodies each second.

items.f: SALIVA ENZYME. It cuts starch in your mouth. Made in a salivary gland cell. Label: E.
items.b: Out of the cell. It works in your mouth, so the gland cell sends it out.

items.f: MILK PROTEIN. Made in the milk gland cells of a mother cow. Label: E.
items.b: Out of the cell. It leaves the cell and becomes part of the milk.

items.f: HAEMOGLOBIN. It carries oxygen. Made in a young red blood cell. No label.
items.b: The watery inside of the cell. With no label, a protein stays where it was made.

items.f: ACTIN. The building block of the thin fibres of the cytoskeleton. No label.
items.b: The watery inside of the cell. Actin filaments are built there.

items.f: TUBULIN. The building block of microtubules. No label.
items.b: The watery inside of the cell. Microtubules are built there.

items.f: KERATIN. The rope protein of skin cells, hair and nails. No label.
items.b: The watery inside of the cell. Keratin ropes stretch across the inside of a skin cell.

items.f: DNA SPOOL PROTEIN. DNA is wound round it. Label: N.
items.b: The nucleus. It is made outside and carried in through a pore.

items.f: DNA-COPYING ENZYME. It copies DNA before a cell divides. Label: N.
items.b: The nucleus. That is where the DNA is.

items.f: A PART OF THE ATP-MAKING MACHINE. Label: M.
items.b: A mitochondrion. Most parts of this machine are made outside and sent in. A few are made inside, from the mitochondrion's own DNA.

items.f: AN ENZYME THAT TAKES FOOD MOLECULES APART TO RELEASE ENERGY. Label: M.
items.b: A mitochondrion. This is where most of the energy in food is passed on to ATP.

items.f: PROTEIN-CUTTING ENZYME that works only in acid. Labels: E and L.
items.b: A lysosome. If the L tag is missing, the cell sends this enzyme out by mistake.

items.f: FAT-CUTTING ENZYME that works only in acid. Labels: E and L.
items.b: A lysosome. It breaks down fats from worn-out membranes.

items.f: INSULIN CATCHER. It sits on the surface of a muscle cell and catches insulin. Labels: E and A.
items.b: The cell membrane. The A part holds it in the membrane, so it stays there.

items.f: SUGAR GATE. A channel that lets sugar into the cell. Labels: E and A.
items.b: The cell membrane. A gate must sit in the membrane to do its work.

items.f: FOLDING HELPER. It helps new proteins fold inside the rough ER. Labels: E and R.
items.b: The ER. The R label brings it back to the ER whenever a vesicle carries it away.

rules: Write the seven places on seven slips of paper and lay them in a row: WATERY INSIDE, NUCLEUS, MITOCHONDRION, OUT OF THE CELL, LYSOSOME, CELL MEMBRANE and ER. Put the label key where everyone can read it.
Shuffle the 18 protein cards and put them in a pile, protein side up.
On your turn, take the top card and read it aloud. Use the key to read its labels. Lay the card under the place you choose.
Turn the card over. If the place is right, you score one point. If not, move the card to the right place.
The game ends when the pile is empty. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: sort all 18 cards, then turn them over. Try to get 15 right.
A harder game for the second time: cover the key, and play from memory.

setup.caption: 1. Lay out the seven places and the label key.

setup.art: A child holding a protein card and running a finger down the label key.
setup.caption: 2. Read the labels on your card and find them on the key.
