flow.do: 1. Cut out the 18 cards and the key. 2. Write the seven place slips and lay them in a row. 3. Read the key aloud once, line by line.
flow.say: A cell makes thousands of kinds of protein. Each one carries a label that says where it belongs. In this game we read the labels, as the cell's machines do.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Lay out the seven places. Read the key aloud once.
flow.parent: The letters are our shorthand. In a real cell, a label is a short stretch of the protein's own chain, or a sugar tag added in the Golgi body.
flow.context: This is the first step of Label Post. Here you lay out the seven places and read the label key.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Read the card aloud. 3. Find its labels on the key. 4. Lay the card under a place. 5. Turn it over to check.
flow.say: Read only the labels. You do not need to know anything else about the protein to send it to the right place.
flow.kid: Take a card. Read its labels. Find them on the key. Lay the card under its place. Check the back.

ask.q: What happens to a protein with no label?
good: It stays in the watery inside of the cell.
Nothing carries it anywhere, so it stays where it was made.

flow.context: This is the main part of Label Post. Here you sort the 18 proteins by their labels.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Pick up one lysosome enzyme card. 3. Cover the L with a finger and ask where the protein goes now. 4. Ask who in the cell would notice the mistake.
flow.say: Suppose this enzyme lost its L tag. Read the key again. Where does the cell send it now?
flow.kid: Count your points. Cover the L on a lysosome card. Where does the protein go now?

check.q: A lysosome enzyme is made without its lysosome tag. Where does the cell send it?
options: To a lysosome anyway
Out of the cell
Back to the nucleus to be corrected
check.why: With only the E label left, the enzyme follows the route out of the cell. This really happens in a rare illness called I-cell disease. Choosing 'to a lysosome anyway' means thinking that something in the cell knows where the enzyme belongs. Only the label says so.

flow.context: This is the last step of Label Post. Here you find out what happens when a label is missing.

experiments.title: The Potato Colour Test: how deep does colour drift in 1 hour, 4 hours and 16 hours?
experiments.context: In this experiment three equal pieces of potato sit in strongly coloured water. You cut one open after 1 hour, one after 4 hours and one after 16 hours. Each time you measure how deep the colour has drifted in.
experiments.question: Colour drifts into a piece of potato with nobody pushing it. If you wait four times as long, does the colour go four times as deep?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After 1 hour you will measure how deep the colour has gone. After 4 hours, will it be the same depth, about twice as deep or about four times as deep? What about after 16 hours? Write your guesses and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the time. Cut all three pieces from one potato, as near the same size as you can. Keep them in the same tumbler of colour, fully covered, in the same place. Measure every piece the same way: on a fresh cut through the middle, at the middle of each of the four sides, away from the corners. At a corner, colour comes in from two sides at once.

materials.item: a large, firm potato (a thick white radish also works)
liquid food colour, red, blue or green. Blue fountain-pen ink, or the juice squeezed from a grated beetroot, also works
a steel tumbler or a glass jar
water
a knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up
a ruler marked in millimetres
a spoon, a plate and an old cloth
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a clock, paper and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Food colour and ink stain cloth and wooden boards, so work on a steel plate and wear old clothes.

schedule.what: Set up the three potato pieces in the colour and write your guesses. Cut and measure one piece after 1 hour and one after 4 hours.
Cut and measure the last piece after about 16 hours. Draw the graph and explain the result.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with all four depths and the mean for each time. Draw a line graph of mean depth against time. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how deep the colour went
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A peeled potato on a chopping board cut into three equal blocks about 3 centimetres long, wide and high, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts three equal blocks from one potato, each about 3 centimetres on every side.

setup.art: Three potato blocks lying under dark red water in a steel tumbler, with a clock beside the tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Cover all three blocks with strong colour. Write down the time.

setup.art: A potato block cut in half, showing a white middle and a coloured rim, with a ruler measuring the rim at the middle of one side.
setup.caption: 3. After 1 hour, 4 hours and 16 hours, cut one block in half and measure the coloured rim in millimetres.

flow.do: 1. Fill a tumbler with water and let it stand still for one minute. 2. Let one drop of colour fall in. Do not stir. 3. Watch for two minutes. 4. Ask what is moving the colour.
flow.say: Nobody is stirring this water. So what is moving the colour? Tell me what you think, and why.
flow.kid: Put one drop of colour in still water. Do not stir. Watch for two minutes. What moves the colour?

ask.q: Nobody stirred. What could be moving the colour?
good: The water is moving a little by itself.
The tiny particles of water and colour are always moving and bumping.

flow.parent: Take any answer for now. In a tumbler, two things move the colour: small currents in the water, and the knocking about of the molecules themselves. Inside a potato, water cannot flow in currents. So the potato shows the second cause alone.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Potato Colour Test. Here you watch a drop of colour spread in still water.

flow.do: 1. Peel the potato. 2. Cut three blocks, each about 3 centimetres long, wide and high. 3. Stir 2 teaspoons of colour into half a tumbler of water. 4. Put the three blocks in and check that the colour covers them. 5. Write down the time.
flow.say: All three pieces come from one potato and are the same size. They go into the same colour at the same moment. Only the time will be different.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts three equal potato blocks. Stir the colour into the water. Put the blocks in. Write down the time.
flow.parent: The colour must be strong: you should not be able to see the spoon through it. If the blocks float, press a small katori down on them. Leave the tumbler where nobody will knock it.
flow.context: This step of the Potato Colour Test sets up the three potato blocks in the coloured water.

flow.do: 1. Explain that one block comes out after 1 hour, one after 4 hours and one after 16 hours. 2. Ask for a guess for the 4 hour block and the 16 hour block, each with a reason. 3. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: After 4 hours, will the colour be as deep as after 1 hour, twice as deep or four times as deep? And after 16 hours? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how deep the colour goes in 4 hours. Guess for 16 hours. Say why. Write it down.

good: Four times as long should give four times as deep, because it keeps going at the same speed.
It might slow down, because the colour has further to go.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Most children, and most grown-ups, expect four times the time to give four times the depth.
flow.context: This step of the Potato Colour Test is for guessing. You guess before any block is cut.

flow.wait: Do this 1 hour after the blocks went in
flow.do: 1. Lift one block out with a spoon. Rinse it for two seconds and pat it dry. 2. Cut it in half through the middle. 3. On the cut face, measure the coloured rim at the middle of each side. 4. Write down the four depths and find the mean.
flow.say: Look at the cut face. The middle is still white. Measure the coloured rim at the middle of each side, in millimetres.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the first block in half. Measure the coloured rim on four sides. Write the four numbers. Find the mean.
flow.parent: After 1 hour the rim is thin, perhaps 1 or 2 millimetres. Judge to the nearest half millimetre, and use a magnifying glass if you have one. Measure to where the colour fades to about half its strength. If the rim is too thin to measure, write 'less than 1' and go on. The 4 hour and 16 hour blocks will still answer the question.
flow.context: This step of the Potato Colour Test comes after 1 hour. Here you cut the first block and measure how deep the colour has gone.

flow.wait: Do this 4 hours after the blocks went in
flow.do: 1. Lift out the second block, rinse it and pat it dry. 2. Cut it in half through the middle. 3. Measure the rim at the middle of each side. 4. Write down the four depths and find the mean.
flow.say: Four hours have passed. Before we cut, remind me of your guess. Now let's measure in the same way as before.
flow.kid: Say your guess again. A grown-up cuts the second block. Measure four sides. Find the mean.

ask.q: Is the colour four times as deep as after 1 hour?
good: No. It is only about twice as deep.
It went further, but much less than four times as far.

flow.parent: Expect about double the 1 hour depth. Anything between one and a half times and three times is normal for a real potato. Do not explain yet.
flow.context: This step of the Potato Colour Test comes after 4 hours. Here you cut the second block and compare it with the first.

flow.wait: Do this the next day, about 16 hours after the blocks went in
flow.do: 1. Lift out the last block, rinse it and pat it dry. 2. Cut it in half through the middle. 3. Measure the rim at the middle of each side. 4. Write down the four depths and find the mean. 5. Look for white potato in the centre.
flow.say: This block had sixteen times as long as the first one. Is the colour sixteen times as deep? Has it reached the centre?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the last block. Measure four sides. Find the mean. Is the centre still white?
flow.parent: Expect about four times the 1 hour depth, and about double the 4 hour depth. The exact time does not matter much now: 15 to 18 hours is fine. If the colour has met in the middle, write 'reached the centre' and compare the 1 hour and 4 hour blocks instead.
flow.context: This step of the Potato Colour Test comes the next day, after about 16 hours. Here you cut the last block.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line graph with time along the bottom and mean depth up the side. 2. Ask your child for the three sentences. 3. Ask the two questions below. 4. Only then read the explanation card on diffusion together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Then tell me this. Is drifting a good way to cross a short distance? Is it a good way to cross a long one?
flow.kid: Draw the graph. Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Each time you waited four times as long. How much deeper did the colour go each time?
good: About twice as deep each time.
The depth doubled when the time became four times as long.

ask.q: A bacterium is about 2 micrometres long, and one of your cells is about 20 micrometres wide. Which one can rely on drifting?
good: The bacterium, because everything in her is very close.
The big cell is ten times as wide, so drifting takes about a hundred times as long.

flow.parent: The graph should rise steeply at first and then bend over. The rule your child may find is this: four times the time gives about twice the depth. The reason is on the diffusion card. A molecule wanders instead of travelling straight, and the Coin Walk activity shows why wandering gives this rule.

check.q: In the Potato Colour Test, colour drifted 2 millimetres into potato in 1 hour. About how long does it need to drift 4 millimetres?
options: About 2 hours
About 4 hours
About 1 hour
check.why: About 4 hours. By drifting, twice as far takes about four times as long. Choosing '2 hours' means thinking that the colour moves at a steady speed, as a walker does. A drifting molecule wanders back and forth, so each extra millimetre takes longer than the one before.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Potato Colour Test. Here you draw the graph and explain your results.

experiments.title: The Fizzing Potato: what do potato cells do to hydrogen peroxide?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put raw, boiled and grated potato into hydrogen peroxide and measure the foam. Hydrogen peroxide is a harmful chemical that all cells make in small amounts. The test shows the enzyme that cells keep in their peroxisomes to destroy it.
experiments.question: Does potato break down hydrogen peroxide? Does it still do so after boiling? Does grating the potato change how fast it happens?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Three glasses hold hydrogen peroxide. One gets a raw potato cube, one a boiled cube and one a raw cube that has been grated. Which glass will fizz most, and which least? Write your guess and the reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the potato. Use the same amount of hydrogen peroxide in each glass, from the same bottle. Cut the three cubes the same size, from the same potato. Start all three at the same moment and measure the foam at the same times.

materials.item: hydrogen peroxide solution, 3 percent, from a chemist's shop
a raw potato
three clear glasses or small glass jars of the same size
a small pan and a stove, to boil one cube
a grater, a knife and a tablespoon
a ruler marked in millimetres
a clock with a seconds hand, or a phone timer

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hydrogen peroxide and does the cutting, grating and boiling. Hydrogen peroxide must not be tasted and must not get into eyes. Rinse it off skin with water. Throw the potato away afterwards.

schedule.what: Boil one potato cube and let it cool. Put a raw cube, the boiled cube and a grated cube into hydrogen peroxide. Measure the foam for 5 minutes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Three equal potato cubes on a plate: one raw, one boiled and steaming in a small pan, and one being grated into a little heap.
setup.caption: 1. Cut three equal cubes. Boil one for 10 minutes and let it cool. Grate one. Leave one raw.

setup.art: Three clear glasses labelled A, B and C, each with the same small amount of clear liquid, and a grown-up's hand pouring from a brown bottle.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up pours 2 tablespoons of hydrogen peroxide into each glass.

setup.art: Three glasses side by side: a raw cube with small bubbles on it, a boiled cube with no bubbles, and grated potato under a thick layer of white foam, with a ruler held against the glass.
setup.caption: 3. Add the potato to all three at once. Measure the foam after 1, 3 and 5 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Cut three cubes of raw potato, each about 2 centimetres on every side. 2. Boil one cube for 10 minutes, then cool it in cold water. 3. Grate the second cube on to a plate. 4. Leave the third cube as it is. 5. Label the glasses A, B and C.
flow.say: We have three equal pieces of the same potato. One is raw, one is boiled and one is grated. What is different about each one?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts three equal cubes. One is boiled. One is grated. One stays raw. Label three glasses A, B and C.
flow.parent: While the cube boils, your child can read the term cards for enzyme and peroxisome. Do not say yet what the potato will do.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fizzing Potato. Here you prepare a raw, a boiled and a grated cube of potato.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the bottle of hydrogen peroxide. 2. Say that every cell makes a little of this chemical and that it harms cells. 3. Ask which glass will fizz most and which least, and why. 4. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Cells make a little hydrogen peroxide as they work, and it harms them. Which potato will fizz most in it: raw, boiled or grated? Which least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which glass will fizz most. Guess which will fizz least. Say why. Write it down.

good: The grated one has the most surface touching the liquid.
Boiling might spoil whatever does the fizzing.
The boiled one is soft, so more might come out.

flow.context: This step of the Fizzing Potato is for guessing. You guess before the potato goes in.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours 2 tablespoons of hydrogen peroxide into each glass. 2. Put the raw cube in A, the boiled cube in B and the grated potato in C, all at the same moment. 3. Start the timer. 4. After 1, 3 and 5 minutes, measure the height of the foam on each glass.
flow.say: Watch all three closely. Where do the bubbles start? Hold the ruler against the glass and measure the foam.
flow.kid: Put the potato in all three glasses together. Start the timer. Measure the foam at 1, 3 and 5 minutes.
flow.parent: The grated potato should foam within a minute. The raw cube makes a slow stream of small bubbles from its surface. The boiled cube makes none, or almost none. If even the grated potato does not fizz, the hydrogen peroxide is too old and has turned to water. Buy a fresh bottle.
flow.context: This step of the Fizzing Potato is the test itself. Here you add the potato and measure the foam.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask the two questions below. 3. Then read the explanation card on peroxisomes together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. What do you think the bubbles are?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: The boiled cube is the same potato. Why did it not fizz?
good: Boiling spoiled something in the potato that makes the fizz.
Heat changes the shape of an enzyme, so it stops working.

ask.q: Why did the grated potato fizz more than the whole cube?
good: Grating breaks open many more cells.
More of the potato touches the liquid, so more enzyme can reach it.

flow.parent: The bubbles are oxygen. Potato cells hold an enzyme called catalase, which turns hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. In a living cell, catalase is kept inside peroxisomes. Be clear with your child: this test shows the enzyme at work, not the peroxisomes themselves, which are far too small to see.

check.q: In the Fizzing Potato test, raw potato made hydrogen peroxide fizz and boiled potato did not. What is the best explanation?
options: Boiling removed the air from the potato
Boiling changed the shape of an enzyme, so it stopped working
Boiled potato is too soft to make bubbles
check.why: The fizz is oxygen, made when the enzyme catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide. An enzyme works only while it has the right shape, and boiling changes that shape. Choosing 'air' means thinking the bubbles were already inside the potato. They are made new, from the hydrogen peroxide.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Fizzing Potato. Here you explain the results.

activities.title: The Coin Walk: wander or walk straight?
activities.context: In this activity a token moves along a paper track. First a coin toss decides each step, forward or back, so the token wanders as a drifting molecule does. Then the token steps forward every time, as a motor protein does. You count the tosses each way needs.

materials.item: a strip of paper about 30 centimetres long
a coin
a small token, such as a button or a rajma bean
a ruler, a pencil and a sheet of paper for the tally

activities.record: Make a table with three rows: wandering to 3 squares away, wandering to 6 squares away, and walking straight to 6 squares away. Write the number of tosses for each run and the mean for each row.

setup.art: A paper strip divided into 13 squares, with the middle square marked START and the squares on each side numbered 1 to 6 going outward.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 13 squares in a row. Mark the middle one START and number 1 to 6 outward on both sides.

setup.art: A child tossing a coin beside the paper strip, with a button on the START square and arrows showing heads to the right and tails to the left.
setup.caption: 2. Toss the coin. Heads, move one square right. Tails, move one square left.

setup.art: A tally sheet with marks counted in fives next to the paper strip, the button now resting on a square numbered 3.
setup.caption: 3. Count the tosses until the token first reaches a square numbered 3. Later, count until it reaches a 6.

flow.do: 1. Draw 13 squares in a row on the strip, each about 2 centimetres wide. 2. Mark the middle square START. 3. Number the squares 1 to 6 outward on both sides. 4. Ask the guessing question below and write the answer down.
flow.say: A coin toss will move the token one square left or right. How many tosses to get 3 squares away from START? And how many for 6 squares? Why?
flow.kid: Draw 13 squares. Mark the middle START. Guess how many tosses to get 3 squares away. Guess for 6 squares. Say why.
flow.parent: Most people guess that 6 squares takes twice as many tosses as 3 squares. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Coin Walk. Here you draw the track and guess.

flow.do: 1. Put the token on START. 2. Toss the coin. For heads move one square right, for tails one square left. 3. Make a tally mark for every toss. 4. Stop when the token first lands on a square numbered 3, on either side. 5. Do 5 runs and find the mean.
flow.say: This is the short trip. Count every toss until the token is 3 squares from START, on either side. We do 5 runs, because single runs differ a lot.
flow.kid: Toss the coin. Heads, go right. Tails, go left. Count the tosses until you reach a 3. Do 5 runs.
flow.parent: The mean is usually near 9 tosses. One run may need only 3 and another 25. That spread is part of the lesson.
flow.context: This step of the Coin Walk is the short trip. Here the token wanders until it is 3 squares from START.

flow.do: 1. Start again from START. 2. This time stop when the token first lands on a square numbered 6, on either side. 3. Tally every toss. 4. Do 5 runs and find the mean. 5. Compare the two means.
flow.say: Now the long trip, twice as far. Before we start, what is your guess now? Count every toss until the token reaches a 6.
flow.kid: Start again. This time go on until you reach a 6. Count the tosses. Do 5 runs. Find the mean.

ask.q: The long trip was twice as far. Did it take twice as many tosses?
good: No, it took about four times as many.
It took far more than twice as many, because the token kept going back.

flow.parent: The mean is usually near 36 tosses, four times the short trip. With only 5 runs, your mean may fall anywhere from about 20 to 60. If the two means are less than three times apart, do 5 more runs of each and find the means of all 10.
flow.context: This step of the Coin Walk is the long trip. Here the token wanders until it is 6 squares from START.

flow.do: 1. Put the token on START once more. 2. Now move it one square to the right for every toss, whatever the coin shows. 3. Count the tosses to reach 6. 4. Compare with the wandering mean.
flow.say: Now the token is a motor protein on a track. Every step goes forward. How many steps to reach 6? Compare that with wandering.
flow.kid: Now step forward every time. Count the steps to reach 6. Compare with wandering.

ask.q: The potato colour needed four times as long to go twice as deep. How does the Coin Walk explain that?
good: A drifting molecule wanders like the token, forward and back.
Twice as far takes about four times as many steps when every step is by chance.

flow.parent: A motor protein reaches square 6 in exactly 6 steps. The wanderer needed about 36. The further the trip, the bigger the gap. This is why a large cell spends ATP on motors and tracks.

check.q: In the Coin Walk, a wandering token needs about 9 tosses to get 3 squares away. About how many to get 6 squares away?
options: About 18
About 36
About 12
check.why: About 36. Twice as far takes about four times as many chance steps, and 4 × 9 = 36. Choosing 18 means doubling, which is right only for a token that steps forward every time.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Coin Walk. Here the token walks straight, as a motor protein does, and you compare the two ways of travelling.

activities.title: A Film That Mends: how a vesicle can join a membrane without a leak
activities.context: In this activity you make a soap film across a bangle and push things through it. You also join two soap bubbles into one. A soap film is a model of a cell membrane: both are thin sheets of molecules that can slide past one another.

materials.item: dish-washing liquid
water
sugar, which makes the film last longer
a wide plate or a shallow bowl
a plain bangle, or a ring made by twisting the ends of a piece of wire together
a drinking straw
a pencil

activities.record: Draw the film with the wet pencil through it. Beside it, draw a vesicle joining a cell membrane. Write one way the film and the membrane are alike, and one way they differ.

setup.art: A bangle being lifted out of a plate of soapy water, with a shining soap film stretched across it.
setup.caption: 1. Dip the bangle in soap solution and lift it out with a film across it.

setup.art: A wet, soapy pencil pushed through a soap film stretched across a bangle, with the film whole all round the pencil.
setup.caption: 2. Push a dry pencil through the film. Then try a pencil wet with soap solution.

setup.art: Two soap bubbles sitting on a wet plate, touching and merging into one larger bubble.
setup.caption: 3. Blow two bubbles on the wet plate and push them together.

flow.do: 1. Stir the dish-washing liquid and the sugar gently into the water in the plate. 2. Dip the bangle flat into the solution and lift it out slowly, so that a film stretches across it. 3. Ask what will happen when a dry pencil is pushed through the film, and why. 4. Push the dry pencil through.
flow.say: This film is far thinner than a hair. What will happen if I push a dry pencil through it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Dip the bangle and lift it slowly. See the film. Guess what a dry pencil will do. Push it through.
flow.parent: The dry pencil bursts the film. If the film will not form at all, add a little more dish-washing liquid and stir without making froth.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Film That Mends. Here you make a soap film across a bangle and push a dry pencil through it.

flow.do: 1. Make a new film. 2. Wet the pencil well in the soap solution. 3. Ask for a guess, then push the wet pencil slowly through the film. 4. Move it about, then pull it out slowly. 5. Try a wet finger.
flow.say: Now the pencil is wet with the same soap solution. What do you think will happen this time? Push slowly and watch the film round the pencil.
flow.kid: Make a new film. Wet the pencil in the solution. Push it slowly through. Pull it out. Did the film break?

ask.q: The pencil made a hole and the film closed again. What does that tell you about the film?
good: The film is liquid, so it flows back and closes the gap.
The soap molecules slide round the pencil and join up again.

flow.parent: The wet pencil passes through and the film stays whole, then closes behind it. The film joins on to the wet soap on the pencil instead of tearing.
flow.context: This step of A Film That Mends pushes a wet pencil through the soap film, to see whether the film can close again.

flow.do: 1. Wet the plate with solution. 2. Dip the straw and blow one bubble on to the plate. 3. Blow a second bubble beside it. 4. Push them gently together with the wet straw until they become one. 5. Read the note below to your child.
flow.say: Watch what happens when two bubbles meet. Do they leak? This is how a vesicle joins the cell membrane and lets its cargo out.
flow.kid: Blow two bubbles on the wet plate. Push them together gently. Watch them become one.

ask.q: A vesicle full of insulin joins the cell membrane. Why does the cell not spring a leak?
good: The two membranes flow into one sheet, as the two bubbles did.
A membrane is liquid, so it closes any gap at once.

flow.parent: Say plainly where the model stops. A cell membrane is two layers of fat-like molecules with water on both sides. A soap film is two layers of soap with water in the middle. So they are built the opposite way round. What they share is that both are liquid sheets, which is why both can join and close without a hole.

check.q: Why can a vesicle join the cell membrane without tearing it?
options: The membrane is a liquid sheet that flows together
The membrane is hard, so it cannot tear
The vesicle makes a hole and the cell leaks a little
check.why: The molecules of a membrane slide past one another, so two membranes that meet can flow into one. Choosing 'hard' means picturing the membrane as a wall. A wall could not let a vesicle join it.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Film That Mends. Here two soap bubbles join into one, as a vesicle joins a cell membrane.

activities.title: Fold It In: how does so much membrane fit in a cell?
activities.context: In this activity you fit a whole sheet of newspaper into a steel tumbler by folding it. The ER and the inner membrane of a mitochondrion are folded in the same way, so that a large area of membrane fits into a small space.

materials.item: a full sheet of newspaper
a steel tumbler
a ruler or a tailor's tape
paper and a pencil

activities.record: Write the area of the newspaper sheet and the area of the tumbler's inside wall. Write how many times bigger the sheet is. Draw the folded sheet inside the tumbler, seen from above.

setup.art: A child measuring the length and width of an open sheet of newspaper on the floor with a tailor's tape.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the newspaper sheet and work out its area.

setup.art: A sheet of newspaper folded into narrow pleats like a paper fan, then rolled and pushed into a steel tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Fold the sheet into a long strip, pleat it like a fan and fit all of it into the tumbler.

setup.art: A steel tumbler seen from above, filled with tightly pleated newspaper, beside a drawing of a mitochondrion with a folded inner membrane.
setup.caption: 3. Look down into the tumbler and compare it with a mitochondrion.

flow.do: 1. Measure the length and the width of the open newspaper sheet in centimetres. 2. Multiply them to find the area. 3. Ask whether the whole sheet can fit inside the tumbler without being torn, and how.
flow.say: A cell needs a great deal of membrane, because much of her chemistry happens on membranes. Can this whole sheet fit in the tumbler? How would you do it?
flow.kid: Measure the newspaper sheet. Multiply length by width. Can it all fit in the tumbler? How?
flow.parent: A full newspaper sheet is about 55 centimetres by 70 centimetres, which is about 4,000 square centimetres. Round the numbers to make the multiplying easy.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fold It In. Here you measure a sheet of newspaper and plan how to fit it into a tumbler.

flow.do: 1. Fold the sheet along its length, again and again, until it is a long strip about as tall as the tumbler. 2. Fold the strip to and fro into pleats about 2 centimetres wide, like a paper fan. 3. Push the pleated strip into the tumbler, standing up. 4. Look down into the tumbler from above.
flow.say: First make a long strip as tall as the tumbler. Then fold it like a fan, with narrow pleats. Now push it in. Look from above. How much paper surface is in there?
flow.kid: Fold the sheet into a long strip. Pleat it like a fan. Push it into the tumbler. Look down from above.

ask.q: The paper is all still there. What did folding change?
good: Only the space it takes up.
The area is the same, but it fits in a small space.

flow.context: This step of Fold It In folds the newspaper into pleats and fits it into the tumbler.

flow.do: 1. Measure round the tumbler and measure its height. 2. Multiply them to find the area of its inside wall. 3. Divide the area of the sheet by the area of the wall.
flow.say: A tumbler with a smooth wall has only this much surface. How many times more did we fit in by folding?
flow.kid: Measure round the tumbler and its height. Multiply them. How many times bigger is the newspaper?
flow.parent: A tumbler about 22 centimetres round and 9 centimetres high has a wall of about 200 square centimetres. The newspaper is about 20 times as big. In a liver cell, the folded ER has much more membrane than the cell's whole outer surface. The folded inner membrane of a mitochondrion has several times the area of her smooth outer membrane.

check.q: Why is the inner membrane of a mitochondrion folded many times?
options: To make the mitochondrion stronger
To fit more ATP-making membrane into a small space
To keep oxygen out
check.why: ATP is made by machines that sit in the inner membrane. More folds mean more membrane, more machines and more ATP in the same small space. Choosing 'stronger' takes the folds for a frame, but they are working surface.

flow.context: This is the last step of Fold It In. Here you compare the area of the folded newspaper with the area of the tumbler's wall.

projects.title: A Cell on a Plate at True Scale, with a bacterium beside her
projects.context: In this two-day project you build a model of one of your cells in which every part has its true size compared with the others. One centimetre in the model stands for one micrometre in the cell. Then you lay a bacterium at the same scale beside the cell.

materials.item: a sheet of newspaper and a plate or lid about 20 centimetres wide, to draw round
a lemon, or a ball of atta dough about 6 centimetres wide
rajma beans, or other beans about 2 centimetres long
whole peppercorns or chana dal
khus khus (poppy seeds) or ragi grains
fine table salt
sewing thread
strips of plain paper, a ruler, a pencil and scissors

schedule.what: Work out the model size of each cell part from its real size. Measure kitchen things to find one of the right size for each part.
Build the cell on the newspaper, lay one bean beside her as a bacterium, and answer three questions about what the model shows.

projects.record: Make a table with four columns: the part, its real size in micrometres, its size in the model, and the thing you used. On the last day write what surprised you most about the sizes.

setup.art: A child measuring a rajma bean, a peppercorn and a lemon with a ruler, beside a table of sizes written on paper.
setup.caption: 1. Work out each model size. Measure kitchen things to find the right ones.

setup.art: A circle 20 centimetres wide drawn on newspaper, with a lemon near the middle, folded paper strips round the lemon, beans scattered about and threads running from near the lemon to the edge.
setup.caption: 2. Build the cell inside a circle 20 centimetres wide.

setup.art: The finished model cell on newspaper with a single rajma bean lying outside the circle, labelled 'bacterium', the same size as the beans inside.
setup.caption: 3. Lay one bean outside the circle. That is a bacterium at the same scale.

flow.do: 1. Copy the list of real sizes from the note below. 2. For each part, write the model size: 1 micrometre becomes 1 centimetre. 3. Measure beans, seeds and other kitchen things with the ruler. 4. Choose the best match for each part and write it in the table.
flow.say: In our model, one micrometre becomes one centimetre. A cell 20 micrometres wide becomes 20 centimetres wide. What size is each part? What in our kitchen is that size?
flow.kid: One micrometre becomes one centimetre. Write the model size of each part. Find a kitchen thing of that size.
flow.parent: Real sizes: the cell is 20 micrometres wide. The nucleus is 6 micrometres wide. A mitochondrion is about 1 micrometre wide and 2 long. A lysosome is about half a micrometre wide. A vesicle is about a tenth of a micrometre wide. A ribosome is a fortieth of a micrometre wide, and a microtubule is just as thick. A common gut bacterium is 1 micrometre wide and 2 long. Good matches are a lemon, rajma beans, peppercorns, khus khus, grains of fine salt and sewing thread.
flow.context: This is day 1 of A Cell on a Plate at True Scale. Here you work out the model size of each part and choose something of that size.

flow.do: 1. Draw round the plate on the newspaper to make a circle 20 centimetres wide. 2. Put the lemon a little off the middle as the nucleus. 3. Fold paper strips to and fro and stand them round the lemon as the ER. 4. Stack five small curved strips as the Golgi body. 5. Scatter 11 beans as mitochondria, peppercorns as lysosomes and khus khus as vesicles. 6. Lay threads from beside the lemon to the edge as microtubules. 7. Sprinkle a little salt as ribosomes.
flow.say: Build the cell inside the circle. The lemon is the nucleus. The beans are mitochondria. The threads are the tracks. The salt grains are ribosomes.
flow.kid: Draw the circle. Put in the lemon. Add folded paper, beans, peppercorns, khus khus, threads and salt.
flow.parent: A real cell of this kind has hundreds of mitochondria and millions of ribosomes, so the model shows the sizes and not the numbers. At this scale the cell membrane would be about as thick as one sheet of paper.
flow.context: This is day 2 of A Cell on a Plate at True Scale. Here you build the cell from kitchen things.

flow.do: 1. Lay the last bean outside the circle and label it 'bacterium'. 2. Ask the three questions below. 3. Move a khus khus seed along a thread at 1 centimetre a second, from the lemon to the edge. 4. Take a photograph of the model, or draw it.
flow.say: This bean is a bacterium at the same scale. What do you notice about her size? Now carry a vesicle along a track at motor speed, one centimetre each second.
flow.kid: Lay one bean outside the circle. She is a bacterium. What do you notice? Move a seed along a thread slowly.

ask.q: The bacterium and a mitochondrion are the same bean. What might that be evidence for?
good: That mitochondria were once bacteria.
They are the same size, and they have other things in common too.

ask.q: Could the whole bacterium fit inside the cell's nucleus?
good: Yes, easily. The nucleus is 6 centimetres wide and the bacterium is 2 centimetres long.

ask.q: Where in the model would drifting be quick, and where slow?
good: Quick inside the bean-sized bacterium.
Slow across the whole 20 centimetre cell, so the cell uses the thread tracks.

flow.parent: A motor protein moves about one micrometre a second, which is one centimetre a second in the model. So the seed takes about 8 seconds from the lemon to the edge.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Cell on a Plate at True Scale. Here you add a bacterium at the same scale and compare.

challenges.title: The Thread Line: carry a parcel along a level track
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In a cell, motor proteins carry vesicles along microtubules, and each step needs energy from ATP. Here you carry a paper parcel of five groundnuts along a level thread 2 metres long, without touching the parcel on the way.
challenges.problem: Stretch a thread 2 metres long between two chairs, level from end to end. A parcel of five groundnuts hangs from a short piece of straw on the thread. Get the parcel from one chair to the other without touching the parcel or the straw after it sets off.
constraints: The thread stays level: both ends at the same height. The parcel may not simply slide downhill.
Nobody touches the parcel or its straw once it has started.
The parcel must arrive with all five groundnuts.
Use only things from the home.
materials: smooth sewing thread or thin string, about 5 metres
five groundnuts in their shells and a small square of paper
a hand fan or a piece of cardboard
general: Tie a second thread to the straw and pull the parcel along from the far chair.
Tape a paper sail to the straw and fan it along.
Flick the thread at one end to shake the parcel forward a little at a time.
creative: Tape a blown-up balloon to the straw and let it go. The air rushing out backward pushes the straw forward.
Make the thread a loop round both chair backs, like a clothes line on two pulleys. Fix the parcel to the loop and pull the other side.
Carry the fuel on board, as a motor protein uses ATP at every step: a wound-up rubber band and a paper propeller on the straw.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own carrier. Draw it, build it and test it 3 times. How long did the best trip take? Where does your carrier get its energy, and where does a motor protein get hers?

setup.art: A thread stretched level between the backs of two chairs 2 metres apart, with a short piece of straw threaded on it and a small paper parcel hanging under the straw.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch a level thread between two chairs. Hang the parcel from a piece of straw on the thread.

setup.art: A blown-up balloon taped along a piece of straw on a level thread, with a paper parcel hanging below and air rushing out of the balloon's neck.
setup.caption: 2. Build a carrier that moves the parcel to the far chair with nobody touching it.

flow.do: 1. Cut a piece of straw 5 centimetres long and pass the thread through it. 2. Tie the thread between two chair backs 2 metres apart, at the same height, and pull it tight. 3. Wrap five groundnuts in paper and tape the parcel under the straw. 4. Give the straw one push and see how far it goes.
flow.say: First let's see what one push does. How far does the parcel get? Why does it stop?
flow.kid: Thread the straw. Tie the thread between two chairs. Tape the parcel under the straw. Give one push.
flow.parent: One push carries the parcel perhaps 30 centimetres before friction stops it. This is the distance to beat. A push at the start is like drifting: it is not enough for a long trip.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Thread Line. Here you set up the level thread and see how far one push takes the parcel.

flow.do: 1. Look at the usual ideas: a pulling thread, a sail and a fan, a flicked thread. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should work. 3. Build it and test it 3 times. 4. Time the best trip.
flow.say: Which idea do you want to try first? Why should it work? Where will the energy come from?
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say why it should work. Build it. Test it 3 times.

ask.q: One push was not enough. What does every idea that works have?
good: Something that keeps pushing or pulling all the way.
A supply of energy during the trip, not only at the start.

flow.context: This step of the Thread Line tests one of the usual ideas.

flow.do: 1. Look at the creative ideas, or invent a new one. 2. Your child draws the design first. 3. Build it and test it 3 times. 4. Compare it with the first idea.
flow.say: Now try an idea where the carrier takes its own energy along. Draw it first. How is it like a motor protein, and how is it different?
flow.kid: Draw your own carrier. Build it. Test it 3 times. Which idea was best?
flow.parent: The balloon works well if the thread is smooth and tight and the balloon is taped along the straw with its neck pointing backward. A balloon gives one long push. A motor protein takes a new sip of energy at every step, which is closer to the pulled loop.

check.q: Where does a motor protein get the energy for each step along a microtubule?
options: From one ATP for each step
From the push of drifting molecules alone
From the microtubule pulling it
check.why: A motor protein uses one ATP for each step. Choosing 'drifting molecules' mixes up the two ways of moving. Drifting costs the cell no ATP, but it goes in no fixed direction. A motor spends ATP and goes one way.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Thread Line. Here you build and test your own carrier.

worksheets.title: Inside a cell: routes, recycling and tracks (core)

items.p: Which part of a cell folds new proteins that are going to leave the cell?
items.why: A protein for export is fed into the rough ER as it is made, and it is folded there. Choosing the nucleus mixes up where the recipe is kept with where the protein is made.

items.p: True or false: a bacterium has ribosomes.
items.why: True. Every living cell builds proteins on ribosomes. A bacterium's ribosomes are a little smaller than yours.

items.p: A ____ is a tiny bubble of membrane that carries cargo inside a cell.
a: vesicle
items.why: A vesicle pinches off from one membrane and joins another. 'Bubble' shows the right idea, but the science word is vesicle.

items.p: Match each cell part to its job.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each part does one main kind of work. A strong answer could also say why the cell needs that work done.
pairs: Golgi body
finishes proteins and sorts them by their labels
Lysosome
digests worn-out parts in acid
Peroxisome
destroys hydrogen peroxide
Microtubule
a track that motor proteins walk along
Smooth ER
makes fats for new membrane

items.p: Put in order the steps by which a protein leaves a cell.
a: A ribosome on the rough ER builds the chain
The chain is folded inside the rough ER
A vesicle carries the protein to the Golgi body
The Golgi body adds sugars and sorts the protein
A vesicle joins the cell membrane and lets the protein out
items.why: The protein is made, folded, carried, finished and sorted, and then sent out. Each step happens in a different place.
items: A vesicle carries the protein to the Golgi body
A vesicle joins the cell membrane and lets the protein out
The chain is folded inside the rough ER
A ribosome on the rough ER builds the chain
The Golgi body adds sugars and sorts the protein

items.p: Sort each of these: found in a bacterium, in your cell or in both.
items.a: see items
items.why: Ribosomes and ATP are things every cell needs. A nucleus and mitochondria are found only in cells like yours. A loose ring of DNA and a wall that penicillin attacks belong to bacteria.
items: main DNA as one loose ring

items.p: In the Potato Colour Test, four times the time gave only about twice the depth. Explain why.
items.a: The colour drifts because its molecules are knocked about in all directions. They wander forward and back and do not travel straight. So each extra millimetre takes longer than the one before, and four times the time gives only about twice the depth.
items.why: A strong answer says that drifting molecules wander, and that this makes the time grow much faster than the distance.

items.p: What happens to a new protein that has no signal label?
opts: It stays in the watery inside of the cell
It is carried into the nucleus
It is sent out of the cell
It is taken to a lysosome
items.why: With no label, nothing carries the protein anywhere, so it stays where it was made. Choosing 'sent out' forgets that export needs a label for the ER.

items.p: Draw a motor protein carrying a vesicle along a microtubule. Label all three.
items.a: A long tube labelled 'microtubule'. On it, a small two-footed protein labelled 'motor protein'. Above the motor, a round bubble much bigger than the motor, labelled 'vesicle'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the motor touching the track with its feet and the vesicle held above. The vesicle should be much bigger than the motor.
items.art: A blank outline of a long tube running across the page.

items.p: A wandering token needs about 9 tosses to get 3 squares away. About how many for 6 squares?
items.why: Twice as far takes about four times as many chance steps. 4 × 9 = 36.

items.p: True or false: a cell builds her microtubules once and keeps them for life.
items.why: False. Most microtubules last only a few minutes. The cell takes them apart and builds new ones, so she can change shape, move and divide.

items.p: Three of these are evidence that mitochondria were once bacteria. Which one is not?
items.why: Their own DNA ring, their own bacteria-like ribosomes and the way they form by splitting are all evidence. Being found in muscle cells says nothing about where they came from.
opts: They have their own ring of DNA
They form only by splitting in two
They are found in muscle cells

items.p: Why is the inside of a lysosome kept acidic?
items.a: The digesting enzymes in a lysosome work well only in acid. The rest of the cell is not acidic. So if some enzyme leaks out, it almost stops working and does little harm to the cell.
items.why: A strong answer gives both parts: the enzymes need acid to work, and this protects the rest of the cell.

items.p: Draw a large animal cell. Draw and label in it: rough ER, Golgi body, lysosome, vesicle and microtubule.
a: Rough ER: folded bags with dots, next to the nucleus
Golgi body: a stack of flat curved bags
Lysosome: a small round bag
Vesicle: a tiny bubble between the Golgi body and the membrane
Microtubule: a long straight line from near the nucleus to the edge
items.why: A strong drawing puts the rough ER beside the nucleus and the Golgi body between the ER and the cell membrane, because that is the route a protein takes.
items.art: A blank outline of a large round cell with a nucleus drawn in.

items.p: Why can a bacterium live without motor proteins and tracks?
opts: She is so small that drifting reaches everywhere quickly
She does not make any proteins
Nothing inside her needs to move
items.why: A bacterium is about 2 micrometres long, and molecules drift that far in a fraction of a second. Choosing 'her nucleus' forgets that a bacterium has no nucleus.

worksheets.title: Inside a cell: labels, fibres and evidence (stretch)

items.p: A cell makes antibodies all day and sends them out. Which part will she have a great deal of?
items.why: Antibodies are proteins for export, so they are made and folded on the rough ER. A cell that exports a lot needs a lot of rough ER.

items.p: In the Fizzing Potato test, grated raw potato foamed much more than a whole raw cube. Explain why.
items.a: Grating breaks open many more potato cells. More of the enzyme catalase can then reach the hydrogen peroxide. So more oxygen is made each second, and there is more foam.
items.why: A strong answer names the enzyme or says 'something in the cells', and says that grating lets more of it meet the hydrogen peroxide.

items.p: Three people talk about whether a bacterium is a 'simple' cell.
items.a: A strong answer uses facts from the unit: no nucleus and no vesicles on tracks, but ribosomes, fibres, fast copying and chemistry that our cells cannot do. It chooses one view and gives a fair point from another.
items.why: Each view is right about something. A bacterium has fewer parts. She also does things our cells cannot. And her size explains why she lives well without a transport system.

views.says: A bacterium is simple. She has no nucleus, no Golgi body and no mitochondria.

views.who: A scientist who studies soil bacteria
views.says: She is not simple. She copies herself in 20 minutes and feeds on things no animal can use.
'Simple' is the wrong word. She is small, and at her size drifting does the carrying.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Give two facts as evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.

items.p: By diffusion, to drift twice as far takes about ____ times as long.
a: four
items.why: A drifting molecule wanders forward and back, so the time grows much faster than the distance. Twice as far takes about four times as long.

items.p: Colour drifts 3 millimetres into a potato in 2 hours. About how many hours does it need to drift 6 millimetres?
items.why: 6 millimetres is twice as far as 3 millimetres. Twice as far takes about four times as long. 4 × 2 = 8 hours.

items.p: Match each label on a protein to the place the cell sends it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The cell's machines read only the label. A strong answer could add that nothing else in the cell knows where the protein belongs.
pairs: No label
stays in the watery inside of the cell
Nucleus label
carried in through a pore of the nucleus
Mitochondrion label
carried into a mitochondrion
ER label alone
through the ER and Golgi body and out of the cell
ER label and lysosome tag
through the ER and Golgi body into a lysosome

items.p: True or false: penicillin harms your cells as much as it harms bacteria.
items.why: False. Penicillin stops bacteria building their cell wall. Your cells have no cell wall, so there is nothing in them for penicillin to stop.

items.p: A cell makes her lysosome enzymes without the lysosome tag. Where do the enzymes go? What happens inside her lysosomes?
items.a: With only the ER label left, the enzymes follow the route out of the cell. The lysosomes are left without their enzymes. So worn-out parts and large molecules pile up in them and are not broken down.
items.why: A strong answer follows the label rule: no lysosome tag means out of the cell. It then says what the lysosomes can no longer do.

items.p: Sort each of these under the right fibre of the cytoskeleton.
items.a: see items
items.why: Actin filaments push and pull the membrane and work with myosin. Microtubules are tracks and pull chromosomes apart. Intermediate filaments are lasting ropes, such as keratin.
items: pushes the front edge of a crawling cell forward
a hollow tube that kinesin walks along
a keratin rope that stops a skin cell tearing
pulled on by myosin in a muscle
pulls the chromosomes apart when a cell divides
what hair and nails are made of

items.p: A nerve cell is one metre long. Why does she not rely on drifting to send vesicles to her far end?
opts: Drifting that far would take hundreds of years
Vesicles are too heavy to float
Drifting only goes towards the nucleus
items.why: The time for drifting grows much faster than the distance. Over a metre it would take hundreds of years. Choosing 'uses too much ATP' has it the wrong way round: drifting costs no ATP, and motors do.

items.p: Draw a mitochondrion and a bacterium side by side. Mark three things they share.
items.a: Two bean shapes of the same size. In each: a ring of DNA and small dots for ribosomes. Other right answers: both make ATP on a membrane, and both multiply by splitting in two.
items.why: A strong drawing makes them the same size and puts the same kind of DNA ring and ribosomes in both. The mitochondrion should have two membranes, with the inner one folded.
items.art: Two blank bean-shaped outlines of the same size, side by side.

items.p: Put in order the steps by which a cell recycles a worn-out mitochondrion.
a: A mitochondrion wears out
A membrane wraps round her
The wrapped parcel joins a lysosome
Enzymes cut her large molecules into small ones
The small molecules are used to build new parts
items.why: This is autophagy. The old part is wrapped, delivered, taken apart and used again.
items: Enzymes cut her large molecules into small ones
The small molecules are used to build new parts
The wrapped parcel joins a lysosome

items.p: A few antibiotics that jam bacterial ribosomes also disturb mitochondria. What does this suggest?
opts: Mitochondria have ribosomes like those of bacteria
Antibiotics jam every ribosome there is
items.why: These antibiotics fit the bacterial kind of ribosome. Mitochondria have their own ribosomes of that kind, which is evidence of where mitochondria came from. The main ribosomes of your cells are not jammed.

items.p: In the Coin Walk, wandering took about six times as many tosses as walking straight. What does this say about large cells?
items.a: Wandering is like drifting, and stepping forward is like a motor protein on a track. Over a long distance, drifting takes far longer than walking straight. So a large cell uses motor proteins and tracks to carry large cargo, even though they cost ATP.
items.why: A strong answer links wandering to drifting and stepping to a motor protein, and says that the gap grows with distance.

items.p: Three of these are in both a bacterium and your cell. Which one is only in your cell?
items.why: Ribosomes, DNA and a cell membrane are in every living cell. A Golgi body is found only in cells with a nucleus, like yours.

worksheets.title: Inside a cell: reasoning from evidence (challenge)

items.p: A bacterium found in 2022 is one centimetre long and keeps her DNA in bags. Use your potato result to suggest why.
items.a: By drifting, twice as far takes about four times as long. A cell one centimetre long is thousands of times longer than an ordinary bacterium, so drifting from one end to the other would take far too long. Keeping DNA and the things that work with it close together in many small bags makes every distance short again.
items.why: A strong answer uses the rule from the potato test and then says how compartments keep distances short. Nobody is yet sure of the full reason, so 'suggest' is the right word.

items.p: Three people talk about what a mitochondrion is.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence from both sides: her own DNA, ribosomes and splitting, and also the genes she has passed to the nucleus and the fact that she cannot live alone. It chooses one view and gives a fair point from another.
items.why: Scientists agree on the facts and differ on the word. The question of when two beings count as one has no agreed answer.

views.says: She has her own DNA and ribosomes, and she comes only from another mitochondrion. She is a living being inside us.
She has given most of her genes to the nucleus and cannot live alone. She is a part of the cell.
Perhaps 'one being or two' has no sharp answer here. She may be something in between.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Give two pieces of evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.

items.p: A scientist cuts the signal stretch off a protein that normally leaves the cell. Where does the protein end up?
opts: In the watery inside of the cell
items.why: Without its signal stretch the protein is never brought to the ER, so it stays where it was made. This experiment is part of the evidence that the address is in the protein itself.

items.p: A motor protein takes 100 steps a second, each 8 millionths of a millimetre. How many millionths in one second?
items.why: 100 steps × 8 = 800 millionths of a millimetre each second. That is a little less than one micrometre a second.

items.p: Many scientists doubted the Golgi body, seen only with silver stain. What evidence settled it, and why was it stronger?
items.a: The electron microscope showed the same stack of flat bags in cells that had not been stained with silver. This was stronger because it was a second, different way of looking. If the stain had made the shape, a method without the stain would not have shown it.
items.why: A strong answer says that a result seen by two different methods is unlikely to be made by either method.

items.p: Sort each statement: shown by strong evidence, or still argued about.
items.a: see items
items.why: The first group rests on many experiments that agree. In the second group, scientists accept the same facts but explain them differently, or the evidence is not yet enough.
items: A protein carries its own address label
The host cell was already large when mitochondria arrived
The bags of the Golgi body themselves move through the stack
Microtubules grow and shrink within minutes
A mitochondrion should be called a living being of her own

items.p: A new medicine stops bacteria building their cell wall. Why should it leave your cells unharmed?
opts: Your cells have no cell wall
Your cells are too big for it
items.why: A medicine that blocks wall-building has nothing to block in a cell with no wall. Choosing 'thicker walls' assumes that animal cells have walls. They have only a membrane.

items.p: Two vesicles reach the cell membrane. Only one has surface proteins that match the membrane. Draw what happens to each.
items.a: One vesicle joined to the membrane and open to the outside, with its matching proteins fitted to the membrane's proteins. The other vesicle still closed and still inside the cell.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that only the vesicle with matching proteins joins. The other does not join, because joining needs the two sets of proteins to fit.
items.art: A curved line for a cell membrane with two small bubbles just inside it.

items.p: True or false: with the right genes in her nucleus, a cell can build a new mitochondrion from nothing.
items.why: False. A new mitochondrion comes only from an older one that grows and splits. The nucleus holds most of the genes, but a mitochondrion must already be there to grow.

items.p: One mitochondrion has a folded inner membrane and another, the same size, a smooth one. Which makes more ATP, and why?
items.a: The one with the folded inner membrane. The machines that make ATP sit in the inner membrane. Folding fits much more membrane into the same space, so there is room for more machines.
items.why: A strong answer says where ATP is made and that folding gives more of that surface. The newspaper in the tumbler showed the same idea.

items.p: A boiled enzyme stops working because heat changes its ____.
a: shape
items.why: An enzyme works by fitting the molecule it changes. Heat changes the enzyme's shape, so the fit is lost.

items.p: Put these in order of size, smallest first.
a: A ribosome
A vesicle
A lysosome
A mitochondrion
A nucleus
A whole skin cell
items.why: In the true-scale model these were a grain of salt, a khus khus seed, a peppercorn, a rajma bean, a lemon and a circle 20 centimetres wide.

items.p: In the Thread Line, one push did not carry the parcel 2 metres. What does a cell do about the same problem?
opts: Her motors use ATP at every step of the way
She pushes cargo once, from the nucleus
She waits for cargo to drift
items.why: A push at the start runs out. A motor protein takes in new energy at each step, so the cargo keeps going for the whole distance.

items.p: Laboratory amoebas came to need bacteria that had infected them. What does this show about mitochondria, and what not?
items.a: It shows that a guest living inside a cell can become a needed partner over many generations. So the first step towards a mitochondrion is possible. It does not show that mitochondria began this way two billion years ago. That evidence comes from their DNA and ribosomes.
items.why: A strong answer separates 'this can happen' from 'this is what happened'. An experiment today can show only the first.

items.p: Match each thing you saw to its explanation.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each result in this unit has a reason at the level of molecules. A strong answer could explain any pair in a full sentence.
pairs: Boiled potato does not fizz
heat changed the shape of an enzyme
Colour goes only twice as deep in four times the time
drifting molecules wander forward and back
A wet pencil passes through a soap film
a liquid sheet closes round a gap
A whole newspaper fits in a tumbler
folding fits a large area into a small space
One bean stands for a bacterium and a mitochondrion
the two are the same size

quiz.p: Colour drifts 1 millimetre into a potato in 10 minutes. About how long does it need to drift 2 millimetres?
quiz.why: Twice as far takes about four times as long, and 4 × 10 = 40 minutes. Choosing 20 minutes means thinking that drifting has a steady speed.

quiz.p: Where in a cell are sugars added to proteins, and proteins sorted into different vesicles?
quiz.why: The Golgi body finishes proteins from the ER and sorts them by their labels. The cytoskeleton carries the vesicles afterwards, but it does not sort them.

quiz.p: Which of these proteins must pass through the rough ER and the Golgi body?
opts: Haemoglobin, which stays in a red blood cell
Actin, which builds fibres in the cell
quiz.why: Insulin does its work outside the cell that makes it, so it takes the export route. The other three stay in the watery inside of the cell.

quiz.p: How does a new protein get to the right place in a cell?
opts: It carries a label that is part of itself
The nucleus sends directions after it
The Golgi body keeps a list of all proteins
It drifts until it finds its place
quiz.why: The address is a short stretch of the protein's own chain, or a tag added to it. Choosing 'the nucleus' or 'a list' imagines a manager, and a cell has none.

quiz.p: A little enzyme leaks out of a lysosome. Why does it do little harm to the cell?
opts: It works well only in acid, and the rest of the cell is not acid
It is too big to move
The rest of the cell has no proteins to cut
quiz.why: Lysosome enzymes need acid. The cell pumps acid into the lysosome, and the rest of the cell is not acid, so a leaked enzyme almost stops working.

quiz.p: True or false: peroxisomes turn hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
quiz.why: True. The enzyme catalase in peroxisomes does this. The oxygen is the fizz you see when raw potato meets hydrogen peroxide.

quiz.p: Which fibre is the main track for carrying vesicles a long way across a cell?
quiz.why: Kinesin and dynein walk along microtubules. Keratin ropes give strength, and no motor walks on them.

quiz.p: Why does a cell keep taking her microtubules apart and building new ones?
opts: So she can quickly change shape, move or divide
Because tubulin is harmful if it is left
quiz.why: A skeleton that is rebuilt every few minutes can be rebuilt in a new arrangement. That lets a cell crawl, change shape and divide.

quiz.p: Which of these does a bacterium not have?
quiz.why: A bacterium is about the size of one mitochondrion. She makes ATP on her own cell membrane. She has the other three, as every living cell does.

quiz.p: A growing cell needs more mitochondria. Where do the new ones come from?
opts: Old mitochondria grow and split in two
quiz.why: New mitochondria come only from older ones, as new bacteria come only from older bacteria. This is one piece of evidence for where mitochondria came from.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: Whether the first host cell was already large
Whether mitochondria have their own DNA
quiz.why: Nobody knows whether the host cell became large before or after mitochondria came to live in her. The other three have been shown many times.

applications: Antibiotics work on the differences between bacterial cells and ours. Penicillin stops bacteria building their wall. Others jam bacterial ribosomes and leave ours working.
Insulin for people with diabetes is made by yeast or bacteria that have been given the human insulin gene. Companies in Bengaluru and Hyderabad make medicines and vaccines this way.

Vincristine, a cancer medicine, comes from the nithyakalyani plant, the pink periwinkle that grows by many Indian roadsides. It stops cells building microtubules, so cells that divide fast can no longer divide.
A few illnesses caused by a missing lysosome enzyme can be treated by giving the enzyme. The medicine carries the lysosome tag, so cells take it in and send it to their lysosomes.
Some vaccines are packed in tiny bubbles of fat, much like vesicles. The bubble joins the cell's own membranes and lets the cargo into the cell.
Doctors clean some wounds with hydrogen peroxide. It foams because catalase from your cells turns it into water and oxygen.
In some nerve illnesses the feet are harmed first. One reason is that the longest nerve cells have the furthest to carry their cargo.

open_questions.q: What was the host cell like when the first mitochondria came to live in her?
open_questions.why_open: It happened about two billion years ago and left almost no fossils. Her living relatives were first grown in a laboratory only in 2020.

open_questions.q: How do proteins move through the Golgi body?
open_questions.why_open: Either vesicles carry them from bag to bag, or the bags themselves move through the stack. Films of living cells support both in different cells.

open_questions.q: How does a cell set the size and the number of her organelles?
open_questions.why_open: A cell keeps roughly the right amount of ER, Golgi body and mitochondria for her size. Nobody has found the full set of signals that does this.

open_questions.q: When a vesicle carries motors that walk in opposite directions, what settles which way it goes?
open_questions.why_open: Some results look like a tug of war. Others suggest the motors take turns. It may differ from cargo to cargo.

open_questions.q: How many partnerships between cells are turning into new organelles today?
open_questions.why_open: The nitrogen-catching organelle in a sea alga was recognised only in 2024. Most single-celled life has never been studied closely.

What in our home gets taken apart so that its pieces can be used again?
Which is quicker for crossing our room: wandering by coin toss, or walking straight? What about crossing one floor tile?
Your mitochondria once lived on their own. Are they you?
Why might a cell want a skeleton she can take apart?
What in our kitchen is folded so that more of it fits in a small space?
Curd bacteria have no nucleus. What do they have that your cells also have?

jokes.a: 'Thanks, but everything I need is one micrometre away.'

jokes.j: What did the vesicle say to the Golgi body?
Why do proteins never get lost?
jokes.a: They never leave the ribosome without their address.

jokes.j: Why did the microtubule fail her exam?
jokes.a: She fell apart after five minutes.

jokes.j: What did the mitochondrion say to the cell?
jokes.a: 'Two billion years I have lived here, and you still call me a guest?'

jokes.j: What did the rough ER say to the smooth ER?

jokes.a: A long walk. One ATP at a time.

Why does the lysosome have no friends for dinner?

maths.problem: In the Potato Colour Test, the coloured rim on the four sides of one block was 3, 4, 5 and 4 millimetres deep. What is the mean depth?
maths.explain: Add the four depths: 3 + 4 + 5 + 4 = 16. Divide by the number of sides: 16 ÷ 4 = 4. So the mean depth is 4 millimetres.
maths.context: This is about the Potato Colour Test. Blocks of potato sit in coloured water, and you measure how deep the colour has gone on each side.
maths.why_maths: The rim is never quite even. The mean of four sides is a fairer number than any one side.

maths.problem: In the Potato Colour Test, the mean depth was 2 millimetres after 1 hour, 4 millimetres after 4 hours and 8 millimetres after 16 hours. What depth do you expect after 64 hours?
maths.explain: Each time the hours are multiplied by 4, the depth is multiplied by 2. From 16 hours to 64 hours is 4 times as long. So the depth doubles from 8 to 16 millimetres. A real potato will be close to this, not exact.
maths.context: This is about the Potato Colour Test, where colour drifts into blocks of potato for 1 hour, 4 hours and 16 hours.

chart.title: Made-up example: how deep the colour went

maths.why_maths: A pattern in the results lets you predict a test you have not done. It also shows that drifting keeps slowing down.

maths.problem: In the Coin Walk, a wandering token needs about 9 tosses to get 3 squares away, and about 36 tosses to get 6 squares away. About how many tosses to get 12 squares away?
maths.explain: The number of tosses is about the distance multiplied by itself. 3 × 3 = 9, and 6 × 6 = 36. So for 12 squares it is 12 × 12 = 144. A token that steps forward every time needs only 12.
maths.context: This is about the Coin Walk, where a token moves left or right by coin toss, as a drifting molecule wanders.
maths.why_maths: Squaring the distance tells you how long wandering takes. It shows why drifting works for tiny distances and fails for long ones.

maths.problem: A motor protein carries a vesicle about 9 centimetres in one day. A nerve cell runs 90 centimetres from a girl's lower back to her toe. How many days does the vesicle take? Drifting would take hundreds of years. Why is the motor so much quicker?
maths.answer: 10 days. The motor steps forward every time, and a drifting vesicle wanders forward and back.
maths.explain: 90 ÷ 9 = 10, so the trip takes 10 days. A motor protein moves about one micrometre each second, always in the same direction. That adds up to about 9 centimetres in a day. A drifting vesicle changes direction all the time, so most of its movement is undone.
maths.context: In the Coin Walk, a token that stepped forward every time reached square 6 in 6 tosses, and a wandering token needed about 36. This problem is about a real motor protein in a long nerve cell.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the distance by the distance covered each day gives the travel time. Then you can compare carrying with drifting.

maths.problem: In the true-scale cell model, 1 micrometre becomes 1 centimetre. That makes everything 10,000 times as big. A child is 130 centimetres tall. How tall would she be at the same scale, in kilometres?
maths.explain: 130 × 10,000 = 1,300,000 centimetres. There are 100 centimetres in a metre, so that is 13,000 metres. There are 1,000 metres in a kilometre, so that is 13 kilometres. One of her cells would be 20 centimetres wide inside a body 13 kilometres tall.
maths.context: This is about the project A Cell on a Plate at True Scale, where a cell is built 20 centimetres wide from kitchen things.
maths.why_maths: Scaling yourself up by the same amount shows how small a cell really is compared with you.

maths.problem: A cell is 10 times as wide, 10 times as long and 10 times as high as a bacterium. How many bacteria would fill the same space? The cell's outer surface is only 100 times as big. Why is that a problem for the cell?
maths.answer: 1,000 bacteria. The cell has 1,000 times as much inside to supply, through only 100 times as much surface.
maths.explain: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000. Surface grows as 10 × 10 = 100. Everything a cell takes in must cross her surface. So each bit of surface of the large cell must serve ten times as much inside. Folded membranes inside the cell, and mitochondria spread all through her, help to solve this.
maths.context: This is about the project A Cell on a Plate at True Scale. A bean 2 centimetres long stood for a bacterium, beside a cell 20 centimetres wide.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying three times for volume and twice for surface shows that a bigger cell is not just a bacterium made larger.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that the Golgi body is real, and what it does? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1898, in the Italian town of Pavia, Camillo Golgi stained nerve cells from a barn owl with silver. Inside each cell he saw a dark net that nobody had described. Other scientists saw it too, but many did not believe it. For fifty years, some of the best cell scientists argued that the net was not a real part of the cell. They said the silver stain itself made it, the way a spilt drink leaves a mark on a table. Light microscopes could not settle the question. In the 1950s the electron microscope could. It showed the net as a neat stack of flat bags in cell after cell, even with no silver stain. Then people asked what it was for. In 1967, James Jamieson and George Palade fed pancreas cells radioactive amino acids for three minutes. They looked for the radioactive proteins at later times. The proteins were first in the rough ER, then in the Golgi body, then in vesicles at the cell's edge. The Golgi body was a station on the route out of the cell.
how_we_found_out.who: Camillo Golgi, who first saw it. Albert Dalton and Marie Felix, who showed it with the electron microscope. James Jamieson and George Palade, who traced proteins through it.
how_we_found_out.when: 1898 (Golgi's silver stain), 1954 (electron microscope pictures) and 1967 (the tracing experiment)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the Golgi body was not a real part of the cell, only a mark made by the silver stain. Electron microscope pictures showed the same stack of bags in cells that had never been stained with silver.
how_we_found_out.art: An old drawing of a nerve cell with a dark net inside it, beside an electron microscope picture of a neat stack of flat bags.

roots.context: We have learned how a large cell ships, recycles and holds her shape, and how a bacterium lives without those parts. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Potato Colour Test, the colour needed four times as long to go twice as deep. Drifting molecules cross a tiny distance quickly and a long distance very slowly. A bacterium is so small that drifting reaches every part of her almost at once. Your cells are about ten times as wide, so they carry large cargo along tracks. Tracks, motors and vesicles are what a large cell needs, and a bacterium lives well without them.
deep_truth.habit: We call a bacterium a simple cell and our own cells advanced, as if she were an unfinished version of us. The potato result shows a different reason for the difference. At her size, drifting does the work that vesicles, tracks and motors do in a large cell.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Potato Colour Test, sixteen times the time gave only about four times the depth. In the Coin Walk, a wandering token needed about four times as many tosses to get twice as far. A giant bacterium found in 2022, one centimetre long, keeps her DNA in membrane bags as large cells do.

three.who_am_i: Each of your cells is large, and she stays alive by carrying cargo along tracks every second. Your mitochondria descend from bacteria who moved into another cell about two billion years ago.
three.what_is_life: Life has more than one design. A bacterium lives by being small, and your cells live by being large and organised inside. Bacteria have lived their way for more than three billion years, and cells like yours for about two billion.
three.what_is_this_world: The same water and the same restless molecules are inside a bacterium and inside you. Size changes what those molecules can do in the time there is.

roots.thread: A bacterium and one of your cells share one ancestor and the same chemistry: DNA, ribosomes, a membrane and ATP. From that one beginning, life found different ways to live at different sizes. Then two different kinds of cell met, and one came to live inside the other. Every animal, plant and fungus has grown from that joining. So the many kinds of life are one family, and some of its branches have joined again.

science.text: Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria that came to live inside larger cells.
The time needed to drift a distance grows with the square of the distance. This limits how large a cell can be without a transport system.
Whether the extra energy from mitochondria is what first allowed cells to become large is still argued.

other_view.view: A cell has no aims and needs nothing. A motor protein steps because ATP changes its shape, and a label is only a patch that sticks to a matching patch. Words like 'needs', 'carries' and 'reads' are a short way of describing chemistry. Nobody inside is doing anything.

practice.title: The longest cell in you
practice.say: Sit with your legs stretched out. Put one hand on your lower back and look at your big toe. A single nerve cell runs all the way from your back to that toe. Wiggle the toe once. The message went down that one cell. Now close your eyes and breathe slowly five times. Inside that long cell, motor proteins are carrying vesicles along microtubules right now. A vesicle that sets off today needs many days to reach your toe. Notice that you do not have to do anything for this to happen.
practice.kid: Sit with your legs out. Put a hand on your lower back. Look at your big toe. One long cell joins them. Wiggle your toe once. Close your eyes and take five slow breaths. Motors are carrying cargo down that cell right now.

ask: If you were as small as a bacterium, which parts of your cells would you still need?
Nobody in a cell directs the traffic, and each protein carries its own label. Who, or what, is organising the cell?
Your mitochondria and your cells cannot live apart any more. When did they stop being two and become one? Did they?

playtest: The experiments and activities in this unit were reasoned through step by step. They have not yet been tried at home, so please treat the amounts and times as a starting point. The Potato Colour Test (core) needs one large potato, strong food colour and two days. The first cut comes after 1 hour, when the coloured rim is only 1 or 2 millimetres deep and hard to measure. If you cannot measure it, compare the 4 hour and 16 hour blocks: the later one should be about twice as deep. Real potatoes give between one and a half and three times, not exactly double. The rim fades at its inner edge, so always measure to where the colour is about half as strong. Weak colour gives a rim too pale to see, so use at least 2 teaspoons in half a tumbler. A grown-up does every cut. The Coin Walk (core) depends on chance, so five runs can give a mean far from 9 or 36. The step says to do five more runs if the two means are less than three times apart. The Fizzing Potato needs 3 percent hydrogen peroxide from a chemist. Old bottles lose their strength: if grated raw potato does not foam, the bottle is the cause. The raw cube makes only a slow stream of bubbles, and the foam layer is clear only on the grated potato. A Film That Mends needs a pencil that is really wet with the soap solution, and still air. Fold It In works with any full newspaper sheet: fold it into a long strip as tall as the tumbler before you pleat it. In A Cell on a Plate at True Scale, measure your own beans and seeds, because sizes vary. In the Thread Line, the thread must be smooth and tight, or the straw sticks. Both games need the cards cut out, and the answer slips and place slips are written by hand. No part needs a garden, a microscope or anything alive except a potato. The three video addresses were confirmed with YouTube on 18 Nov 2026, but the videos were not watched from here. The numbers for drifting times in cells are rounded estimates, and the two teachings in Roots are paraphrases.
